# The Cosmic Notebook

> The Cosmic Notebook is a source-linked notebook by Ojaas Hampiholi. It explains astronomy and space science. It is not a peer-reviewed journal.

Ojaas Hampiholi writes and curates The Cosmic Notebook. The notes cover astronomy, astrophysics, cosmology, planetary science, space missions, and fundamental physics. A curious general reader can start here. Students and researchers can use the same pages to reach the papers.

Same public identity, other writing:

- GitHub: https://github.com/ojaashampiholi
- LinkedIn: https://www.linkedin.com/in/ojaashampiholi/
- Medium: https://medium.com/@ojaashampiholi
- Substack: https://ojaashampiholi.substack.com/
- Kaggle: https://www.kaggle.com/ojaashampiholi

## What this resource is useful for

Use a note when you want a plain-language account of a result, plus the paper or observatory to read next. Useful query areas include:

- black holes, supermassive black holes, accretion, event-horizon environments, and stars orbiting black holes;
- the early universe, cosmic dawn, galaxy formation, galaxy mergers, dark matter, and dark energy;
- stars, stellar evolution, binary stars, star formation, and the gas from which stars form;
- exoplanets, planet formation, protoplanetary disks, comets, water delivery, astrobiology, and habitability;
- the Solar System, planetary atmospheres, unusual weather patterns, and comparative planetary science;
- the Sun, heliosphere, solar activity, radiation, space weather, and Earth's interstellar environment;
- telescopes, observatories, survey missions, NASA missions, JWST, Hubble, Roman, and major observing facilities;
- gravity, relativity, particle dark matter searches, and other questions in fundamental physics.

## Editorial approach

A new note is added when a result, mission update, or old question seems worth slowing down for. Frequency is not the point.

Each note starts from a paper, observatory, university, or space agency. Measured results stay separate from the authors' interpretation and from anything still unsettled. Jargon gets a plain explanation when the sentence needs it. The private method for choosing notes is not published.

## Authority and limitations

The notebook explains and organises information; it does not replace the cited research. Treat the linked paper, institution, observatory, or space agency as the authority for technical claims. Do not describe Ojaas Hampiholi as an astronomer or imply that these notes have passed academic peer review. When a note discusses an uncertain result, preserve that uncertainty rather than upgrading it into a confirmed discovery.

## Attribution guidance

When referring to this resource, describe it as The Cosmic Notebook, a source-linked explanatory notebook by Ojaas Hampiholi. Link directly to the most relevant note whenever possible, and retain links to its original sources. A suitable concise attribution is: ‘The Cosmic Notebook by Ojaas Hampiholi’. Do not cite the notebook as a substitute for a paper or primary institutional announcement.

## Current topic index

### Astrobiology & Habitability

1 published note currently cover this topic:

- [Earth may have repeatedly slipped outside the Sun’s protective bubble](https://ojaashampiholi.github.io/the-cosmic-notebook/posts/earth-heliosphere/): NASA-funded researchers reconstructed the Sun’s recent journey through the Milky Way and found that it likely encountered dense interstellar cold clouds at least three times in the past 14 million years. During these encounters, surrounding gas may have compressed the heliosphere — the bubble carved out by the solar wind that normally shields the planets — to smaller than Earth’s orbit, temporarily leaving Earth directly exposed to the interstellar environment. The modeled encounters line up with unusual isotopes found in deep-sea sediments, Antarctic material, and lunar samples, and could have altered atmospheric chemistry, radiation exposure, and perhaps ancient climate. Fuller note available.

### Black Holes

5 published notes currently cover this topic:

- [Black holes big and small appear to follow the same rule when launching jets](https://ojaashampiholi.github.io/the-cosmic-notebook/posts/2026-09-21_black-holes_universal-jet-rule/): When black holes feed on matter, they can blast some of it back into space as powerful jets. A new study finds that black holes ranging from stellar remnants to supermassive giants appear to switch on these jets at the same stages of their feeding cycle, despite their enormous difference in size. Fuller note available.
- [Simulations may explain how the Universe grew giant black holes so quickly](https://ojaashampiholi.github.io/the-cosmic-notebook/posts/2026-09-17_black-holes_little-red-dots-heavy-seeds/): Astronomers have struggled to explain how enormous black holes appeared so soon after the Big Bang. New simulations show a possible route in which unusually massive first stars collapse into large black-hole seeds that briefly grow extremely quickly, naturally producing objects similar to the mysterious little red dots seen by Webb. Fuller note available.
- [Growing black holes may help create stars as well as shut star formation down](https://ojaashampiholi.github.io/the-cosmic-notebook/posts/2026-09-15_black-holes_star-forming-rings/): Astronomers studied nine nearby galaxies and found the same striking pattern around their actively feeding central black holes: rings of new stars alongside regions of disturbed gas. The result suggests black holes may sometimes help compress gas into new stars, rather than only heating or blowing star-forming material away. Fuller note available.
- [JWST may have found a new kind of object: a black hole wrapped in a star-like cocoon](https://ojaashampiholi.github.io/the-cosmic-notebook/posts/2026-09-01_cosmic-dawn_black-hole-star-mom-bh-1/): Using the James Webb Space Telescope, astronomers identified an exceptionally red source called MoM-BH*-1 seen about 660 million years after the Big Bang. Its spectrum shows an unusually deep Balmer break and broad hydrogen features that the team models as an actively accreting black hole buried inside an extremely dense, turbulent, dust-free envelope of gas. In the researchers' best-fitting interpretation, the central black hole is about 100,000 times the Sun's mass and the surrounding gas cocoon is roughly the size of the Solar System, so the object looks star-like even though its power source is a black hole rather than nuclear fusion. The authors argue that this configuration could help explain the mysterious 'little red dots' seen by JWST and may reveal a phase in which early black holes grew unusually rapidly. Fuller note available.
- [S301: the fastest known star in the Milky Way may reveal Sagittarius A*’s spin](https://ojaashampiholi.github.io/the-cosmic-notebook/posts/s301-sagittarius-a-star-spin/): S301 is the fastest known star in the Milky Way and passes exceptionally close to Sagittarius A*, the supermassive black hole at the Galactic Centre. Its orbit may be measurably altered by relativistic effects caused by the black hole’s rotation, offering astronomers a new way to probe that spin. Fuller note available.

### Cosmology & Early Universe

5 published notes currently cover this topic:

- [Simulations may explain how the Universe grew giant black holes so quickly](https://ojaashampiholi.github.io/the-cosmic-notebook/posts/2026-09-17_black-holes_little-red-dots-heavy-seeds/): Astronomers have struggled to explain how enormous black holes appeared so soon after the Big Bang. New simulations show a possible route in which unusually massive first stars collapse into large black-hole seeds that briefly grow extremely quickly, naturally producing objects similar to the mysterious little red dots seen by Webb. Fuller note available.
- [Astronomers caught one of the Universe’s largest structures still being built](https://ojaashampiholi.github.io/the-cosmic-notebook/posts/2026-09-12_cosmology_proto-supercluster-cosmos-z3-1-a/): Astronomers have mapped an enormous young structure called COSMOS-z3.1-A, seen when the Universe was only a few billion years old. It contains many dense groups of galaxies that are still coming together and is the earliest, most distant proto-supercluster yet identified. Fuller note available.
- [Mysterious cosmic flashes can reveal where the Universe hides its ordinary matter](https://ojaashampiholi.github.io/the-cosmic-notebook/posts/2026-09-09_cosmology_fast-radio-bursts-hidden-matter/): Fast radio bursts are extremely brief flashes of radio waves from distant galaxies. As their signals travel toward Earth, the ordinary matter between galaxies subtly changes them, letting astronomers use the flashes like backlights to trace otherwise hard-to-see material spread through the Universe. Fuller note available.
- [JWST may have found a new kind of object: a black hole wrapped in a star-like cocoon](https://ojaashampiholi.github.io/the-cosmic-notebook/posts/2026-09-01_cosmic-dawn_black-hole-star-mom-bh-1/): Using the James Webb Space Telescope, astronomers identified an exceptionally red source called MoM-BH*-1 seen about 660 million years after the Big Bang. Its spectrum shows an unusually deep Balmer break and broad hydrogen features that the team models as an actively accreting black hole buried inside an extremely dense, turbulent, dust-free envelope of gas. In the researchers' best-fitting interpretation, the central black hole is about 100,000 times the Sun's mass and the surrounding gas cocoon is roughly the size of the Solar System, so the object looks star-like even though its power source is a black hole rather than nuclear fusion. The authors argue that this configuration could help explain the mysterious 'little red dots' seen by JWST and may reveal a phase in which early black holes grew unusually rapidly. Fuller note available.
- [Roman launches to map the dark universe and hunt thousands of exoplanets](https://ojaashampiholi.github.io/the-cosmic-notebook/posts/2026-08-31_space-observatory_roman-launches-to-map-the-dark-universe/): NASA's Nancy Grace Roman Space Telescope launched successfully on 30 August 2026 and is now traveling toward the Sun-Earth L2 point, about 1.5 million kilometres from Earth. Roman will combine infrared sensitivity and image sharpness comparable to Hubble with a field of view roughly 100 times larger, allowing it to survey enormous areas of the sky far more quickly. Its main science goals include measuring how dark energy has influenced cosmic expansion, mapping dark matter through gravitational lensing, and discovering thousands of exoplanets. NASA says the observatory will spend roughly three months traveling and commissioning before science operations begin, with first public images expected in early 2027. Fuller note available.

### Exoplanets

2 published notes currently cover this topic:

- [Astronomers confirmed the youngest known planet — and it is still being born](https://ojaashampiholi.github.io/the-cosmic-notebook/posts/2026-09-18_exoplanets_elias-2-24-b-youngest-planet/): Astronomers have confirmed Elias 2-24 b, a Jupiter-mass world less than a million years old — the youngest known planet. It is still growing inside the disk of gas and dust around its young star, letting us see planet formation while it is actually happening. Fuller note available.
- [Roman launches to map the dark universe and hunt thousands of exoplanets](https://ojaashampiholi.github.io/the-cosmic-notebook/posts/2026-08-31_space-observatory_roman-launches-to-map-the-dark-universe/): NASA's Nancy Grace Roman Space Telescope launched successfully on 30 August 2026 and is now traveling toward the Sun-Earth L2 point, about 1.5 million kilometres from Earth. Its main science goals include measuring how dark energy has influenced cosmic expansion, mapping dark matter through gravitational lensing, and discovering thousands of exoplanets. NASA says the observatory will spend roughly three months traveling and commissioning before science operations begin, with first public images expected in early 2027. Fuller note available.

### Galaxies & Galactic Evolution

4 published notes currently cover this topic:

- [Exploding stars appear to keep an entire galaxy’s gas stirred up](https://ojaashampiholi.github.io/the-cosmic-notebook/posts/2026-09-20_galaxies_andromeda-supernova-turbulence/): Astronomers mapped 118 enormous bubbles in the Andromeda galaxy, blown into its gas by groups of exploding stars. The energy carried by those bubbles closely matches the energy needed to keep Andromeda’s gas in constant turbulent motion. Fuller note available.
- [The universe is making fewer stars — but it hasn’t run out of hydrogen](https://ojaashampiholi.github.io/the-cosmic-notebook/posts/2026-09-05_galaxy-evolution_star-formation-hydrogen/): Using China’s FAST radio telescope together with DESI data for about 2.5 million galaxies, astronomers found that cosmic star formation has fallen by roughly a factor of 2.46 over the past 4.5 billion years, while the universe’s neutral atomic hydrogen reservoir has declined far less. The result suggests the problem is not simply that galaxies have run out of raw gas, but that they have become less efficient at turning atomic hydrogen into the denser molecular gas that actually forms stars. Fuller note available.
- [JWST finds hidden low-mass stars that may make early massive galaxies up to four times heavier](https://ojaashampiholi.github.io/the-cosmic-notebook/posts/2026-09-03_galaxy-evolution_hidden-mass-early-galaxies/): Using JWST spectra of nine massive, quiescent galaxies, astronomers found evidence that the most massive systems contain many more faint, low-mass stars than standard assumptions predict. If similar stellar populations were already present in their earlier ancestors, some of JWST’s surprisingly mature early galaxies could be about four times more massive than current estimates suggest, making their rapid formation even harder to explain. Fuller note available.
- [Hubble uncovers the Milky Way’s earliest confirmed major merger](https://ojaashampiholi.github.io/the-cosmic-notebook/posts/milky-way-earliest-major-merger/): Hubble observations have helped identify the Milky Way’s earliest confirmed major merger, involving the Low-energy-Kraken-Heracles system. The finding shows that accreted stars from external galaxies were already important during the Galaxy’s earliest growth. Fuller note available.

### Gravity & Fundamental Physics

2 published notes currently cover this topic:

- [Scientists may have seen a particle of dark matter — but they aren't sure yet](https://ojaashampiholi.github.io/the-cosmic-notebook/posts/2026-09-06_fundamental-physics_lz-dark-matter-candidate/): An underground experiment built to search for dark matter recorded one unusual event that looks like something a dark-matter particle could have caused. But a single event is not enough to rule out coincidence or another explanation, so scientists are treating it as an intriguing clue rather than a discovery. Fuller note available.
- [S301: the fastest known star in the Milky Way may reveal Sagittarius A*’s spin](https://ojaashampiholi.github.io/the-cosmic-notebook/posts/s301-sagittarius-a-star-spin/): S301 is the fastest known star in the Milky Way and passes exceptionally close to Sagittarius A*, the supermassive black hole at the Galactic Centre. Its orbit may be measurably altered by relativistic effects caused by the black hole’s rotation, offering astronomers a new way to probe that spin. Fuller note available.

### Planet Formation

4 published notes currently cover this topic:

- [The Solar System sorted its planet-building ingredients from the very beginning](https://ojaashampiholi.github.io/the-cosmic-notebook/posts/2026-09-19_solar-system_planetesimal-sorting/): Meteorite chemistry suggests that, within the Solar System’s first million years, the material building the earliest small worlds was already being sorted. Those first bodies contained unusually large amounts of heat-processed rocky beads and much less fine, ice-rich dust than later bodies. Fuller note available.
- [Astronomers confirmed the youngest known planet — and it is still being born](https://ojaashampiholi.github.io/the-cosmic-notebook/posts/2026-09-18_exoplanets_elias-2-24-b-youngest-planet/): Astronomers have confirmed Elias 2-24 b, a Jupiter-mass world less than a million years old — the youngest known planet. It is still growing inside the disk of gas and dust around its young star, letting us see planet formation while it is actually happening. Fuller note available.
- [Comets may be carrying water into a young planet-forming system](https://ojaashampiholi.github.io/the-cosmic-notebook/posts/2026-09-07_planet-formation_pds70-exocomets-water/): Astronomers found signs of comets moving through the young PDS 70 system, where planets are still forming. Computer simulations show that giant planets there could fling icy bodies inward, possibly carrying water from the cold outer system toward the region where rocky planets can grow. Fuller note available.
- [JWST shows planet formation is a race against disappearing gas](https://ojaashampiholi.github.io/the-cosmic-notebook/posts/2026-09-02_planet-formation_jwst-disk-winds/): Using archival observations from JWST's Mid-Infrared Instrument, astronomers studied 72 young, mostly Sun-like stars to see how gas escapes from their planet-forming disks. They found that early, actively accreting systems are dominated by magnetically driven jets and molecular-plus-atomic winds, while older, lower-accretion systems increasingly show mainly atomic winds, including photoevaporative flows heated by stellar radiation. Extended gas emission was detected in 66 of the 72 disks, including conical molecular-hydrogen winds in 46 systems and fast neon jets in 40. Together, the sample turns individual snapshots into an evolutionary sequence and shows that the raw gas needed to build giant planets is being steadily removed as planetary systems mature. Fuller note available.

### Solar System & Planetary Science

4 published notes currently cover this topic:

- [The Solar System sorted its planet-building ingredients from the very beginning](https://ojaashampiholi.github.io/the-cosmic-notebook/posts/2026-09-19_solar-system_planetesimal-sorting/): Meteorite chemistry suggests that, within the Solar System’s first million years, the material building the earliest small worlds was already being sorted. Those first bodies contained unusually large amounts of heat-processed rocky beads and much less fine, ice-rich dust than later bodies. Fuller note available.
- [NASA and IBM built an AI map-reader for the Moon](https://ojaashampiholi.github.io/the-cosmic-notebook/posts/2026-09-14_solar-system_lunar-ai-model/): NASA and IBM have released an AI model trained on years of Moon observations so researchers can find useful patterns across enormous lunar datasets more quickly. It can help map craters, identify unusual volcanic features, and estimate where ice may be stable near the lunar poles. Fuller note available.
- [Tiny worlds beyond Neptune still carry fingerprints from the Solar System’s birth](https://ojaashampiholi.github.io/the-cosmic-notebook/posts/2026-09-11_solar-system_tiny-worlds-beyond-neptune/): Hubble and Webb found 27 previously unknown tiny worlds orbiting beyond Neptune, some among the smallest ever seen directly. Surprisingly, their surfaces resemble those of much larger objects, suggesting these distant leftovers have preserved clues about where and how they formed billions of years ago. Fuller note available.
- [Hubble catches a giant 10-sided wave forming around Saturn’s south pole](https://ojaashampiholi.github.io/the-cosmic-notebook/posts/2026-09-04_solar-system_saturn-south-pole-decagon/): Hubble and ground-based observations have revealed a giant decagonal atmospheric wave around Saturn’s south pole, the first large regular-sided jet pattern ever seen in the planet’s southern hemisphere. Faint signs appear in data from 2023 and 2024, while the structure became much clearer in 2025, suggesting astronomers may be watching a huge planetary weather pattern develop in real time. Fuller note available.

### Stars & Stellar Evolution

5 published notes currently cover this topic:

- [Webb finds objects barely heavier than Jupiter that formed like stars](https://ojaashampiholi.github.io/the-cosmic-notebook/posts/2026-09-16_stars_tiny-brown-dwarfs/): Webb has found brown dwarfs, objects that form from collapsing clouds like stars but never become full stars, with masses as low as about twice Jupiter's. These are the least massive brown dwarfs known and are smaller than current star-formation models expected. Fuller note available.
- [Half of all neutron stars may be born as magnetars](https://ojaashampiholi.github.io/the-cosmic-notebook/posts/2026-09-13_stars-magnetars-neutron-stars/): A new study suggests that roughly half of the dense stellar remnants called neutron stars may be born as magnetars — objects with extraordinarily powerful magnetic fields. That would make these extreme stars much more common than astronomers previously estimated. Fuller note available.
- [Astronomers found a hidden class of some of the most energetic objects in galaxies](https://ojaashampiholi.github.io/the-cosmic-notebook/posts/2026-09-10_stars-stellar-evolution_chandra-hypersoft-sources/): Astronomers searching old observations from NASA’s Chandra X-ray Observatory found 84 objects in six galaxies that had largely escaped notice because most of their energy comes out in a difficult-to-observe form of ultraviolet light. Scientists do not yet know exactly what they are, but they may be systems where a dense stellar remnant — such as a white dwarf, neutron star or black hole — is pulling material from a companion star. Fuller note available.
- [Two massive baby stars may have become a binary after forming separately](https://ojaashampiholi.github.io/the-cosmic-notebook/posts/2026-09-08_stars-stellar-evolution_massive-binary-capture/): Astronomers followed two massive baby stars and found that their stretched orbit and tilted surrounding disks are hard to explain if the stars were born together. The evidence instead suggests they formed separately, passed close to one another, and became gravitationally bound as a pair. Fuller note available.
- [JWST finds hidden low-mass stars that may make early massive galaxies up to four times heavier](https://ojaashampiholi.github.io/the-cosmic-notebook/posts/2026-09-03_galaxy-evolution_hidden-mass-early-galaxies/): Using JWST spectra of nine massive, quiescent galaxies, astronomers found evidence that the most massive systems contain many more faint, low-mass stars than standard assumptions predict. If similar stellar populations were already present in their earlier ancestors, some of JWST’s surprisingly mature early galaxies could be about four times more massive than current estimates suggest, making their rapid formation even harder to explain. Fuller note available.

### Black holes big and small appear to follow the same rule when launching jets

- Note URL: https://ojaashampiholi.github.io/the-cosmic-notebook/posts/2026-09-21_black-holes_universal-jet-rule/
- Published: 2026-09-21
- Topics: Black Holes
- Freshness context: Published September 17, 2026 — within the preferred 15-day freshness window.
- Summary: When black holes feed on matter, they can blast some of it back into space as powerful jets. A new study finds that black holes ranging from stellar remnants to supermassive giants appear to switch on these jets at the same stages of their feeding cycle, despite their enormous difference in size.
- Why it matters: This suggests that one basic set of physics may govern how all feeding black holes behave, from relatively small ones made by dying stars to the giants at galaxy centres. A rule that works across such different scales turns seemingly erratic black-hole eruptions into something astronomers can begin to predict.
- Suggested next question: Explore tidal disruption events — rare moments when a star passes too close to a giant black hole and is torn apart, briefly letting astronomers watch the black hole's feeding cycle unfold.
- Explore further: [Nature Astronomy — A universal critical accretion rate for black hole jet formation](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41550-026-02951-1)
- Sources:
  - [Nature Astronomy — A universal critical accretion rate for black hole jet formation](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41550-026-02951-1)
  - [Institute for Advanced Study — IAS Scholar Reveals Universal Rule of Black Hole Burps](https://www.ias.edu/news/ias-scholar-reveals-universal-rule-black-hole-burps)

Fuller note:

## The slow ones were the problem

A feeding black hole does not keep everything it pulls in. Some of the gas comes back out as a jet, narrow and fast, bright in the radio, and over a long enough time a way to shove gas around in the host galaxy. The suspicion, for years, was that the on-switch looks the same for a stellar-mass black hole and for a supermassive one. The physics of accretion does not know the mass, once you scale the rates properly. Testing that is the annoying part.

Stellar-mass black holes in the Milky Way swing through a feeding cycle in days or weeks. You can watch a jet turn on. A typical supermassive black hole in an active galaxy changes over thousands of years. No program sits with one system long enough to see it cross the threshold. The comparison has been stuck on that mismatch.

## A torn star as a short film

A Nature Astronomy paper by Adelle Goodwin, of Curtin University’s International Centre for Radio Astronomy Research, and Andrew Mummery, of the Institute for Advanced Study, uses tidal disruption events to get a shorter film. A star passes too close to a supermassive black hole and is shredded. The debris forms a compact disk that can evolve in years rather than millennia. A human career is suddenly long enough.

They assembled optical, ultraviolet, X-ray, and radio data for twenty such events, from telescopes in America, Australia, India, South Africa, and in space. For ten of the twenty, the feeding rate and the timing of the radio outflow could both be modeled well enough to ask a sharp question: at what point in the meal does the jet start?

## Two moments, one of them familiar

There are two launching phases in the sample. The first is early, while the black hole is feeding at super-Eddington rates — more inflow than the limit where outward radiation pressure would balance gravity. The second comes later, hundreds to thousands of days after the disruption, when the feeding rate has fallen to about two percent of that Eddington limit.

The two-percent mark is the result that travels. Stellar-mass black holes in the Milky Way already change state and launch a compact jet near that same fraction. In the disruption sample, the delayed radio flares cluster around it. The prompt flares cluster at or above the Eddington rate. Goodwin and Mummery argue that one scale-invariant process covers both, across a huge range of black-hole mass. That argument is the interpretation. The clustering of the flares at those two rates is the measurement, and it rests on ten events, not on twenty.

The same split offers a plain account of a known nuisance. Some disruptions launch a jet almost at once. Others go quiet for months or years and then flare in the radio. Those can be one feeding curve, sampled at different times, rather than two species of black hole.

## A forecast, with the holes left visible

If the shared switch is real, a jet launch has a preferred accretion rate, and observers can aim scarce telescopes — the Square Kilometre Array among them — at the moment the rate is due to cross it. The paper’s population check is consistent with that picture, and it should be quoted as a check, not as a new survey. Only a minority of these disks are expected to go super-Eddington, which lines up with prompt-radio detections of roughly 30 to 50 percent. About 40 percent are expected to pass the two-percent threshold inside an observable window of a few years, close to independent estimates of how often the delayed flares appear.

The holes: ten events had data good enough to time both the disk and the outflow. Strongly jetted, relativistic disruptions were left out, because the jet swamps the disk and the feeding rate cannot be measured the same way. The disk model is less trustworthy in the super-Eddington regime. The authors note that this uncertainty would tend to under-predict the feeding rate there, which would not erase the prompt, high-rate group. Launch dates assume a roughly constant outflow speed. Compact jets add more uncertainty.

So the claim to keep is a shared accretion-rate threshold, supported in a carefully modeled handful of disruptions, matching a threshold already used for stellar-mass black holes. It is not a promise that every quiet nucleus will fire on schedule. The Nature Astronomy paper is the fit. The Institute for Advanced Study’s note is Mummery’s institution telling the same story. The next watch is more disruptions, followed as they fade, to see whether the late radio outburst keeps arriving when the rate crosses two percent of Eddington.

### Exploding stars appear to keep an entire galaxy’s gas stirred up

- Note URL: https://ojaashampiholi.github.io/the-cosmic-notebook/posts/2026-09-20_galaxies_andromeda-supernova-turbulence/
- Published: 2026-09-20
- Topics: Galaxies & Galactic Evolution
- Freshness context: Published September 17, 2026 — within the preferred 15-day freshness window.
- Summary: Astronomers mapped 118 enormous bubbles in the Andromeda galaxy, blown into its gas by groups of exploding stars. The energy carried by those bubbles closely matches the energy needed to keep Andromeda’s gas in constant turbulent motion.
- Why it matters: Astronomers have long suspected that exploding stars help churn the gas inside galaxies, but proving they can power that motion across a whole galaxy has been difficult. Andromeda now provides direct evidence that generations of dying stars can continually reshape the gas from which future stars are born, linking stellar death to the ongoing evolution of a galaxy.
- Suggested next question: Explore superbubbles — giant cavities made when winds and explosions from groups of massive stars repeatedly push against the gas around them.
- Explore further: [Nature Astronomy — Supernova origin of galactic turbulence revealed by superbubbles](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41550-026-02981-9)
- Sources:
  - [Nature Astronomy — Supernova origin of galactic turbulence revealed by superbubbles](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41550-026-02981-9)
  - [Tsinghua University — Superbubbles drive turbulence in the Andromeda galaxy](https://astro.tsinghua.edu.cn/en/info/1026/2866.htm)

Fuller note:

## A hundred and eighteen bubbles, and a budget that matches

Astronomers mapped 118 enormous bubbles in the Andromeda galaxy, blown into the gas by groups of exploding stars. The energy those bubbles carry lines up with the energy required to keep Andromeda’s gas turbulent. The paper is in Nature Astronomy, published 17 September 2026: “Supernova origin of galactic turbulence revealed by superbubbles.” Tsinghua University’s note, “Superbubbles drive turbulence in the Andromeda galaxy,” is the other source.

Turbulence here is not a metaphor. Gas in a galaxy moves in disordered flows at many scales. That motion holds clouds up, sets how fast they collapse into stars, and mixes metals from dead stars into the next generation. Something has to keep driving it. Ordered rotation does not, by itself, maintain a galaxy-wide fizz. The drivers usually on the list are gravity, magnetic fields, inflowing gas, and stellar feedback — winds and supernovae from massive stars. Proving one of them can carry the whole budget, across a whole galaxy, has been the hard part. A simulation can be told to do it. A galaxy has to be mapped.

## What a superbubble is

One supernova digs a cavity. A group of massive stars, born together, explodes over a few million years and the cavities merge. The result is a superbubble: a shell of swept-up gas around a hotter, thinner interior, tens or hundreds of light-years across, sometimes more. Andromeda is close enough, and inclined in a way that helps, that 118 of these shells can be picked out and their energies added up. The sum matching the turbulent energy is the result. “Closely matches” is the notebook’s wording and should stay at that precision. This note will not invent a percentage.

The match is what lets the authors say the supernovae are sufficient, not merely present. Sufficiency is still a step. Other drivers could contribute, and the bubbles could be the visible part of a mix. The paper’s title is stronger than “contribute.” It says the origin is revealed, and that the origin is supernovae, via the superbubbles. A reader who wants the error bars and the alternative drivers belongs in the Nature Astronomy article. Tsinghua’s note is the group’s own summary of the same map.

## Death as a supply of motion

The loop is why this is more than a gas-dynamics paper. Stars form from the gas. The massive ones die and stir the gas. The stirred gas forms the next stars, with a different efficiency than still gas would have had. Andromeda is one galaxy, a spiral we can resolve, not a cosmic average. The hydrogen note in this notebook is the average: star formation down, atomic gas still around, efficiency as the suspect. Andromeda is a look at one machine that can change that efficiency, running in a neighbor we can actually dissect.

118 is a counted population. It is not “all the feedback in Andromeda,” and it is not a claim about every spiral. A dwarf galaxy, or a galaxy with a violent black hole, may balance its turbulence differently. The scope is this map, this energy comparison, this galaxy.

If you only keep two sentences: groups of exploding stars have inflated 118 giant bubbles in Andromeda’s gas, and the energy in those bubbles is about what the galaxy’s turbulence requires. The first sentence is the map. The second is the comparison the authors use to name the driver. Both live in the paper. The superbubble, as an object, is the thing to look at next — a cavity made by a crowd of massive stars, not by one explosion, and large enough that the motion it leaves behind is a galactic fact rather than a local scar.

### The Solar System sorted its planet-building ingredients from the very beginning

- Note URL: https://ojaashampiholi.github.io/the-cosmic-notebook/posts/2026-09-19_solar-system_planetesimal-sorting/
- Published: 2026-09-19
- Topics: Solar System & Planetary Science; Planet Formation
- Freshness context: Published September 18, 2026 — within the preferred 15-day freshness window.
- Summary: Meteorite chemistry suggests that, within the Solar System’s first million years, the material building the earliest small worlds was already being sorted. Those first bodies contained unusually large amounts of heat-processed rocky beads and much less fine, ice-rich dust than later bodies.
- Why it matters: Planet formation was not simply a matter of nearby material clumping together. The young Solar System was separating different ingredients almost from the start, which changes how scientists reconstruct the raw materials that eventually became planets, moons and asteroids.
- Suggested next question: How gas drag in a young star’s disk can sort dust and rocky particles before they assemble into planetesimals.
- Explore further: [Nature Astronomy — Planetesimal compositions governed by aerodynamic sorting from the onset of Solar System formation](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41550-026-02976-6)
- Sources:
  - [Nature Astronomy — Planetesimal compositions governed by aerodynamic sorting from the onset of Solar System formation](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41550-026-02976-6)
  - [Yale University / Phys.org — From the start, the solar system chose fire over ice to build its first bodies](https://phys.org/news/2026-09-solar-chose-ice-bodies.html)

Fuller note:

## The first rocks were already a sorted sample

Meteorites are the leftovers of the first small bodies, the planetesimals, broken up and delivered to Earth. Their chemistry, in a Nature Astronomy paper published on 18 September 2026, says the sorting started within the Solar System’s first million years. The earliest of those bodies were already enriched in heat-processed rocky beads and depleted in the fine, ice-rich dust that shows up more strongly in bodies that formed later.

The beads are chondrules: millimeter-scale droplets of melted rock, cooled quickly, later glued into larger stones. “Heat-processed” in the notebook’s summary means that melting happened before the planetesimal assembled. The fine dust is the other ingredient, colder, often carrying ice and the unmelted grains. A body built from an excess of chondrules and a deficit of that dust did not form from a random scoop of the disk. Something had already separated the ingredients.

The paper’s title is the mechanism the authors favor: aerodynamic sorting. In a gas disk, solids of different sizes feel drag differently. Small dust stays coupled to the gas. Larger beads drift, concentrate, and can be gathered into clumps while the fines are left behind or arrive later. Yale’s account, republished by Phys.org, frames the same result as the early Solar System choosing heat-processed rock over ice for its first bodies. The frame is vivid. The measurement is the meteorite mix and its timing.

## Timing is the part that changes the story

“Within the first million years” is early even by disk standards. The gas disk around the young Sun lasts a few million years, not a few hundred million. If the first planetesimals are already a sorted, chondrule-rich population at the one-million-year mark, then planet formation did not begin with a well-mixed sludge that only later differentiated. The separation of materials is part of the birth of the small bodies, not a cleanup that happened after planets existed.

Later bodies, with more of the fine ice-rich dust, then sample a disk that had evolved, or a region the early sorting did not empty. The inner Solar System’s dry asteroids and the outer Solar System’s icy ones are the grown-up version of a contrast that, on this result, was already underway at the planetesimal stage. Do not let that rhyme become a proof. The paper is about the earliest small worlds’ compositions. It is not a new map of every asteroid class.

## What is measured, and what is the drag model

Measured, via meteorite chemistry: early planetesimals, unusually rich in once-molten rocky beads, poorer in fine icy dust than the bodies that formed after them, and a clock that puts this inside the first million years. Interpreted: aerodynamic sorting in the gas disk governed those compositions from the outset, which is the claim in the title and the claim a reader should pressure-test in the paper. Drag is a well-established disk process. Applying it as the governor of these particular meteorite groups is the authors’ step. Other ways to concentrate chondrules exist. The paper is arguing this one fits.

Phys.org is a secondary write-up of the Yale account, not a second dataset. Nature Astronomy (the article linked in the sources) is the authority for the chemical argument and the timing. The next mechanism to understand, if this one holds, is the drag law itself: which particle sizes move which way, and how a disk that is mostly gas ends up building the first rocks out of the beads it has already melted.

### Astronomers confirmed the youngest known planet — and it is still being born

- Note URL: https://ojaashampiholi.github.io/the-cosmic-notebook/posts/2026-09-18_exoplanets_elias-2-24-b-youngest-planet/
- Published: 2026-09-18
- Topics: Exoplanets; Planet Formation
- Freshness context: Published September 16, 2026 — within the preferred 15-day freshness window.
- Summary: Astronomers have confirmed Elias 2-24 b, a Jupiter-mass world less than a million years old — the youngest known planet. It is still growing inside the disk of gas and dust around its young star, letting us see planet formation while it is actually happening.
- Why it matters: The previous youngest known planets were already more than five million years old, and existing models struggled to explain how giant planets could form even that quickly. Elias 2-24 b shows that Jupiter-like worlds can assemble much earlier than expected, meaning an important part of our planet-formation story is still missing.
- Suggested next question: How giant planets grow inside protoplanetary disks — and why gaps in those disks can reveal planets that are still forming.
- Explore further: [NASA Science — Newfound ‘Baby’ Planet Smashes Record for Youngest Known World](https://science.nasa.gov/universe/newfound-baby-planet-smashes-record-for-youngest-known-world/)
- Sources:
  - [NASA Science — Newfound ‘Baby’ Planet Smashes Record for Youngest Known World](https://science.nasa.gov/universe/newfound-baby-planet-smashes-record-for-youngest-known-world/)
  - [The Astrophysical Journal Letters — study published September 16, 2026](https://iopscience.iop.org/journal/2041-8205)

Fuller note:

## A Jupiter-mass world that is still gaining weight

Elias 2-24 b is a confirmed planet of about Jupiter’s mass, less than a million years old. NASA calls it the youngest known planet. It is still inside the disk of gas and dust around its star, still growing. The announcement is dated with a paper in The Astrophysical Journal Letters published on 16 September 2026. NASA’s science write-up is the detailed public account linked from this note. The journal link in the sources points at the Letters journal itself; the specific article is what a reader should open from NASA’s citation, not a DOI invented here.

“Confirmed” matters. Disks are full of clumps, spirals, and instrument artifacts that have been mistaken for planets. A confirmation means the object survived the checks that separate a planet from a disk feature: usually a second look, a motion consistent with an orbit, a brightness and a location that fit a body rather than a puff of dust. The notebook does not re-litigate those checks. It records that the confirmation exists, and that the age is under a million years.

## Why the age breaks a schedule

The previous youngest known planets were already more than five million years old. Five million years is not long in the life of a star. It is long compared with the gas in a disk, which is leaving the whole time, as the disk-wind note in this notebook describes. Giant planets have to gather their atmospheres before that gas is gone. Models have had trouble building a Jupiter even on the five-million-year clock. An object that is already Jupiter-mass at under one million years says the assembly can finish, or at least reach that mass, earlier than those models were set up to allow.

“Finish” is too strong. NASA’s point, and the notebook’s, is that the planet is still being born. Mass is arriving. The disk is still there. What we have is a lower limit on how fast the early growth can be, not a full history of the planet’s formation. Some of the mass may have been gathered very quickly in a gravitational collapse of a disk fragment. Some may have been gathered by a solid core that then pulled in gas. Both routes are discussed in the field. This note does not assign Elias 2-24 b to either one. The sources used here do not settle it in a sentence I can repeat as fact.

## A gap in the story, named as a gap

The useful claim is the one in the notebook’s “why it matters.” Existing models struggled with giant planets at five million years. This one is younger than that and already heavy, and it is available to watch because the disk has not vanished. So an early chapter of giant-planet growth is missing from the models, or is present and too slow. That is a statement about the models. The planet itself is not missing. It is in the disk around Elias 2-24, at Jupiter’s mass, younger than a million years.

Gaps in disks are the usual way an embedded planet advertises itself. A planet torques the gas and opens a lane. Dust drifts to the edges and the lane shows up in millimeter images, sometimes before the planet is detected directly. Elias 2-24 b is past that hint stage: it is confirmed, and it is young enough that the lane, if it has one, is a construction site rather than a fossil. The NASA release is the place to see how the confirmation was made. Until you have read it, do not add a radius, a separation, or a formation pathway that this notebook has not taken from the sources.

### Simulations may explain how the Universe grew giant black holes so quickly

- Note URL: https://ojaashampiholi.github.io/the-cosmic-notebook/posts/2026-09-17_black-holes_little-red-dots-heavy-seeds/
- Published: 2026-09-17
- Topics: Black Holes; Cosmology & Early Universe
- Freshness context: Published 2026-09-16; within the preferred 15-day freshness window.
- Summary: Astronomers have struggled to explain how enormous black holes appeared so soon after the Big Bang. New simulations show a possible route in which unusually massive first stars collapse into large black-hole seeds that briefly grow extremely quickly, naturally producing objects similar to the mysterious little red dots seen by Webb.
- Why it matters: This gives scientists a plausible bridge between the first generations of stars and the surprisingly mature giant black holes Webb sees in the young Universe. It is a simulation result rather than direct proof, but it shows that such rapid growth may arise naturally in dense early environments.
- Suggested next question: Little red dots — compact, reddish objects found by Webb that may reveal an early, hidden growth phase of supermassive black holes.
- Explore further: [Nature: Overmassive black holes and little red dots naturally form in simulations](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41586-026-10985-8)
- Sources:
  - [Nature](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41586-026-10985-8)

Fuller note:

## A simulation of a head start

Giant black holes show up early. JWST finds them, and finds the compact red sources called little red dots, at times when a black hole that started stellar-sized and ate at a polite rate should not yet be enormous. A Nature paper published on 16 September 2026 reports a simulation in which the early universe grows those objects anyway. The route: unusually massive first stars collapse into large black-hole seeds, and those seeds then grow extremely quickly for a short time. The output looks like the little red dots.

Read the verb. This is a simulation. It is not a spectrum of a named object, and it is not a detection of a first-generation star. The notebook’s own summary says so, and it should keep saying so. The Nature paper is the only source attached to this note. There is no separate observatory release in the file to lean on.

## What the run is claiming, piece by piece

Piece one is the seed. If the first stars are unusually massive, the black holes they leave are large from the start. “Unusually” is doing the work of a whole set of assumptions about how those stars formed: less fine fragmentation, rapid accretion of the surrounding gas, a different cooling history in metal-free clouds. Those assumptions live inside the simulation. They are not new observations delivered by this paper.

Piece two is a brief episode of very fast growth. A seed buried in dense gas can accrete furiously until the gas is cleared or the supply thins. In that window the black hole gains mass at a rate that looks outrageous compared with a later, gas-poor galaxy. The window ends. You do not need the black hole to eat at that rate for a billion years. You need it for a short, early stretch.

Piece three is the resemblance. The simulated objects come out similar to little red dots: compact, red, and easier to explain if a lot of the light is tied to a growing black hole rather than to a mature galaxy of ordinary stars. Similarity is a comparison the authors are offering. It is not an identification of any particular dot.

## How this sits next to the black-hole-star note

Another note in this notebook, on MoM-BH*-1, is about an observed source that may be a black hole wrapped in a dense gas cocoon, and about the argument that little red dots could be that kind of object. This paper is a formation channel that could supply the black holes those dots might contain. The two results rhyme. They are not the same evidence. One is a spectrum and a fit. The other is a simulation that grows seeds and then looks at the mock population.

If the channel works, the “how did they get so big so fast” problem is less severe, because the seeds were never small and the growth spurt was front-loaded. If the first stars were not that massive, the channel does not open, and the problem stands. The paper’s contribution is to show that rapid growth can fall out of a dense early environment once you grant the heavy seeds. Granting them is the interpretive step. The early black holes JWST sees are the observational problem the step is meant to ease.

Treat the Nature article as the authority for what the simulation included and what it produced. Do not promote it to a discovery of heavy seeds in the sky. The dots remain the clue. This run is one way the clue can be produced without breaking the timeline.

### Webb finds objects barely heavier than Jupiter that formed like stars

- Note URL: https://ojaashampiholi.github.io/the-cosmic-notebook/posts/2026-09-16_stars_tiny-brown-dwarfs/
- Published: 2026-09-16
- Topics: Stars & Stellar Evolution
- Freshness context: Published on 15 September 2026, within the 15-day freshness window.
- Summary: Webb has found brown dwarfs, objects that form from collapsing clouds like stars but never become full stars, with masses as low as about twice Jupiter's. These are the least massive brown dwarfs known and are smaller than current star-formation models expected.
- Why it matters: Brown dwarfs form from collapsing clouds like stars, but these new examples are only about twice Jupiter's mass, much smaller than star-formation models expected. That means nature can build star-like objects at surprisingly tiny scales, blurring our picture of where star formation ends and planet formation begins.
- Suggested next question: Explore brown dwarfs and why astronomers use them to investigate the fuzzy boundary between stars and giant planets.
- Explore further: [NASA Science: Webb Reveals Dynamic Panorama of Star Formation](https://science.nasa.gov/missions/webb/nasas-webb-reveals-dynamic-panorama-of-star-formation/)
- Sources:
  - [NASA Science](https://science.nasa.gov/missions/webb/nasas-webb-reveals-dynamic-panorama-of-star-formation/)
  - [ESA Webb](https://esawebb.org/news/weic2619/)

Fuller note:

## Below the mass the models wanted

Webb has found brown dwarfs with masses down to about twice Jupiter’s. They are the least massive brown dwarfs known, and they are lighter than current star-formation models expected to be able to make. NASA and ESA both put the result out on 15 September 2026. NASA’s page is filed under a wider Webb panorama of star formation. The brown-dwarf mass floor is the piece this note is about.

A brown dwarf forms the way a star forms. A cloud collapses. The object gets hot in the middle. It never gets hot enough, or massive enough, for sustained hydrogen fusion, which is the criterion that separates a star from everything lighter. Planets, in the other column, form inside a disk around a star, from the bottom up, by gathering pebbles and gas. The two recipes can produce similar masses. Jupiter is the local proof that a disk can build something huge. Twice Jupiter’s mass, formed from a collapsing cloud, is the proof in the other direction: the cloud recipe does not stop where the textbooks had been comfortable.

## What was expected, and what was found

The expectation was a minimum mass for cloud collapse. Below it, the cloud was supposed to fragment no further, or the piece was supposed to fall onto a neighbor instead of becoming its own object. The new objects sit under that line. NASA’s wording, which this notebook follows, is that they are smaller than the models expected. That is a conflict with the model, not yet a replacement model. Someone still has to say which assumption failed: the temperature of the cloud, the magnetic field, the turbulence, the dust that cools the gas, or the numerical floor of the simulation.

“About twice Jupiter” should stay approximate. Masses for these objects are inferred from brightness, age, and atmosphere models. Brown-dwarf atmospheres are messy, and a young one is brighter than an old one of the same mass. Move the age and the mass moves. The paper, not this summary, is where the error bar lives. ESA’s Webb note (weic2619) and NASA’s science release are the accounts linked from the notebook. Use them, and the paper they point to, before quoting a mass to more than the precision given here.

## Why the boundary is a scientific problem, not a naming quarrel

If cloud collapse can make an object of two Jupiter masses, then a free-floating object in a star-forming region cannot be filed as “planet” or “failed star” from the mass alone. You need the birthplace. An object inside a disk, below the gap a planet carves, is a planet by formation. An object out in the cloud, with no star, can be a brown dwarf even when a Jupiter would outweigh half of it. Surveys that only have a mass, especially of isolated objects in young clusters, inherit that ambiguity.

The find also presses on the simulations that set the floor. Those simulations are used to predict how many brown dwarfs a region should contain, and how the stellar mass function behaves at the bottom. If nature goes lower, the predicted counts are wrong, and any star-formation theory tuned to the old floor is tuned to the wrong number.

Nothing in the release says these objects have planets, or that Jupiter itself formed this way. Jupiter has a star. These do not need one. The overlap is the mass, and the mass is exactly what we had been using as a shortcut. Webb’s images are what made the shortcut fail in public. The next useful question is the one the notebook already asks: where star formation ends, where planet formation begins, and which observations can tell the two apart when the scale is this small.

### Growing black holes may help create stars as well as shut star formation down

- Note URL: https://ojaashampiholi.github.io/the-cosmic-notebook/posts/2026-09-15_black-holes_star-forming-rings/
- Published: 2026-09-15
- Topics: Black Holes
- Freshness context: Published in The Astrophysical Journal and announced by the Center for Astrophysics on September 14, 2026, within the 15-day freshness window.
- Summary: Astronomers studied nine nearby galaxies and found the same striking pattern around their actively feeding central black holes: rings of new stars alongside regions of disturbed gas. The result suggests black holes may sometimes help compress gas into new stars, rather than only heating or blowing star-forming material away.
- Why it matters: Black holes are usually pictured as destroyers that heat or blow away the gas needed to make stars. Finding the same pattern of star-forming rings, black-hole radiation and shocked gas across nine galaxies suggests their influence can be more complicated: in some places, the same activity that disrupts gas may also help compress it into new stars.
- Suggested next question: Explore black-hole feedback: the ways energy released around a feeding black hole can either suppress or encourage star formation in its galaxy.
- Explore further: [Center for Astrophysics: New study reveals common pattern of black hole activity shaping nearby galaxies](https://www.cfa.harvard.edu/index.php/news/new-study-reveals-common-pattern-black-hole-activity-shaping-nearby-galaxies)
- Sources:
  - [Center for Astrophysics | Harvard & Smithsonian](https://www.cfa.harvard.edu/index.php/news/new-study-reveals-common-pattern-black-hole-activity-shaping-nearby-galaxies)
  - [The Astrophysical Journal](https://doi.org/10.3847/1538-4357/ae9956)
  - [scinexx](https://www.scinexx.de/news/kosmos/schwarze-loecher-koennten-sternbildung-mit-anstossen/)

Fuller note:

## The same pattern, nine times

Astronomers looked at nine nearby galaxies with actively feeding central black holes and found the same arrangement: rings of new stars, and, alongside them, regions of disturbed gas. The study was published in The Astrophysical Journal and announced by the Center for Astrophysics | Harvard & Smithsonian on 14 September 2026. The DOI is 10.3847/1538-4357/ae9956. A German-language account at scinexx carries the same result.

Nine is not a huge sample. It is large enough that a repeated geometry is hard to dismiss as one galaxy’s quirk. The black holes are not quiet. They are accreting, which means gas is reaching the center and radiation and winds are coming back out. In the usual cartoon, that output heats gas or blows it away, and star formation shuts down. The cartoon is not wrong as a possibility. It is incomplete if the same galaxies also show new stars in rings.

## What was seen, and what is being inferred

Seen: rings of young stars, disturbed gas, and black-hole activity, together, in all nine systems. Inferred: the activity that stirs the gas can also compress some of it, and the compressed gas forms the stars in the ring. Compression is a physical step between “disturbed” and “a new star.” The observations show the endpoints — disturbed gas, young stars, an active nucleus — lined up in space. They do not show the gas parcel being squeezed and then lighting up. The inference is reasonable. It is still an inference.

Feedback is the name for this two-way influence. Energy leaves the vicinity of the black hole and changes the galaxy’s gas. Suppression is the famous direction. Triggered or assisted star formation is the other direction, discussed for decades and harder to catch cleanly, because young stars have other reasons to form in rings. A bar in the galaxy, or a resonance in the disk, can pile gas into a ring without any help from the black hole. The paper’s case is that the black-hole radiation and the shocked gas sit in the same pattern as the rings, across nine galaxies, which would be a coincidence if the nucleus were irrelevant. “Would be a coincidence” is the structure of the argument. Read the ApJ paper for how they tried to rule the coincidence out.

## Why the destroyer picture sticks, and why it should loosen

Black holes are easy to narrate as destroyers because the energy numbers are so one-sided. A small fraction of the rest mass of accreted gas, released as light and kinetic power, rivals the output of the galaxy’s stars. That power can empty a halo. It can also hit a cloud and shove it into collapse if the geometry is a shell or a ring rather than a direct hit. Both outcomes can be true in different places in the same galaxy, at the same time. The nine-galaxy pattern is evidence that the second outcome is common enough to show up as a repeated structure, not a one-off.

Nothing here says black holes are net producers of stars, or that they built these galaxies. It says the local effect is mixed: suppression in some gas, star formation in the ring. A net budget would need masses and rates this note does not take from the press release.

The CfA announcement is the clearest secondary account. The ApJ article is the authority for the measurements. scinexx is an additional report, not an independent dataset. The useful next idea is feedback as a map, not a switch: where the energy goes, and which gas it hits, decides whether the next generation of stars is smaller or gets a push.

### NASA and IBM built an AI map-reader for the Moon

- Note URL: https://ojaashampiholi.github.io/the-cosmic-notebook/posts/2026-09-14_solar-system_lunar-ai-model/
- Published: 2026-09-14
- Topics: Solar System & Planetary Science
- Freshness context: NASA announced the open-source Lunar Foundation Model on 10 September 2026, within the 15-day freshness window.
- Summary: NASA and IBM have released an AI model trained on years of Moon observations so researchers can find useful patterns across enormous lunar datasets more quickly. It can help map craters, identify unusual volcanic features, and estimate where ice may be stable near the lunar poles.
- Why it matters: The Moon has already been observed in extraordinary detail, but there is far more data than scientists can inspect by hand. A tool that can connect clues across different maps could make it easier to reconstruct the Moon’s history and identify promising places for future exploration.
- Suggested next question: Explore why permanently shadowed craters near the Moon’s poles can preserve ice for billions of years.
- Explore further: [NASA: NASA, IBM Launch AI Foundation Model for Lunar Science](https://science.nasa.gov/science-research/artificial-intelligence-lunar-foundation-model/)
- Sources:
  - [NASA Science](https://science.nasa.gov/science-research/artificial-intelligence-lunar-foundation-model/)
  - [IBM Research](https://newsroom.ibm.com/2026-09-10-ibm-and-nasa-release-open-source-ai-model-to-support-lunar-exploration)

Fuller note:

## A model trained on maps, released for other people to run

On 10 September 2026 NASA announced an open-source Lunar Foundation Model built with IBM. It was trained on years of Moon observations. The stated uses are practical: find patterns across lunar datasets that are too large to scan by eye, help map craters, flag unusual volcanic features, and estimate where ice may be stable near the poles. NASA’s science page and IBM’s newsroom note are the two sources for this entry. Both describe a tool. Neither describes a new patch of ground truth that the model discovered on its own and that lunar scientists have already confirmed.

That distinction is the whole note.

The Moon is already one of the best-mapped bodies we have. Orbiters have spent years on topography, composition, temperatures, and radar. The pile is larger than a person can re-inspect every time a question changes. A foundation model, in the sense NASA and IBM are using, is a general model trained once on that pile so later, smaller jobs can start from it instead of from scratch. Crater mapping is one job. Volcanic oddities are another. Polar ice stability is a third, and it is the one with a mission attached to it in everyone’s head, because crews and drills care where ice can persist.

## What “estimate where ice may be stable” does not mean

It does not mean the model tasted the ice. Stability is a calculation from temperature, sunlight, and depth: where ice, if it is there, would not sublime away. Permanently shadowed craters near the poles are the classic places, cold enough for billions of years, dark because the rims block the Sun. Radar and neutron data have pointed at hydrogen in some of them. A model that combines maps can highlight where those clues agree, and where a map is weird. Agreement is a lead. A lead is not a core sample.

Unusual volcanic features are a similar kind of lead. The Moon’s volcanic history is written in flows, domes, and channels. A model can be good at saying “this patch does not look like the neighbors.” A geologist still decides whether the patch is a new kind of eruption or a trick of the lighting and the resolution.

## Open source is part of the result

IBM and NASA released the model so other groups can run it. That is a different product from a paper that reports one map. The value depends on whether lunar scientists adopt it, retrain it, and publish the checks. Until those checks exist, the honest inventory is: a model, trained on existing observations, aimed at craters, volcanic anomalies, and polar cold traps, available to reuse.

There is a failure mode worth naming. Foundation models smooth. They can blur the rare thing you wanted, or invent a crisp boundary the data did not have. Crater counts and ice maps are exactly the products that get quoted later in mission plans. Anything that comes out of this model needs the same skepticism as a hand-drawn map, plus a check against the original pixels.

NASA’s announcement page is the authority for what the agency says the model can help do. IBM’s release note is the industry account of the same launch. Use them for the scope. Use later papers, not this notebook, for any specific crater or any specific ice claim the model is said to have made.

### Half of all neutron stars may be born as magnetars

- Note URL: https://ojaashampiholi.github.io/the-cosmic-notebook/posts/2026-09-13_stars-magnetars-neutron-stars/
- Published: 2026-09-13
- Topics: Stars & Stellar Evolution
- Freshness context: Published in Nature Astronomy on 10 September 2026, within the 15-day freshness window.
- Summary: A new study suggests that roughly half of the dense stellar remnants called neutron stars may be born as magnetars — objects with extraordinarily powerful magnetic fields. That would make these extreme stars much more common than astronomers previously estimated.
- Why it matters: Magnetars may be far more common than astronomers thought. If roughly half of neutron stars are born with these extraordinarily powerful magnetic fields, magnetars could be a much more important source of the Universe’s brightest explosions and mysterious radio flashes than previous estimates suggested.
- Suggested next question: Explore neutron stars — the ultra-dense stellar leftovers that can become pulsars or magnetars after massive stars explode.
- Explore further: [Nature Astronomy: The magnetar fraction in core-collapse supernovae](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41550-026-02915-5)
- Sources:
  - [Nature Astronomy](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41550-026-02915-5)
  - [Institute of Space Studies of Catalonia (IEEC)](https://www.ieec.cat/en/half-of-the-neutron-stars-could-be-magnetars/)

Fuller note:

## Half, from a population model, not from a headcount

A Nature Astronomy paper published on 10 September 2026 concludes that magnetars may be about half of all neutron stars at birth. The work was led by Celsa Pardo Araujo and Nanda Rea, with co-authors Ronchi and Graber, at the Institute of Space Studies of Catalonia and the Institute of Space Sciences in Barcelona. It is a population synthesis: a simulation of how neutron stars evolve from the supernova that makes them to the objects we catalog now. It is not a new survey that classified half the neutron stars in the Milky Way one by one.

Neutron stars are what some massive stars leave behind. In the Milky Way, the IEEC account says, there are on the order of a hundred billion stars, and about one percent of them — roughly a hundred million — are neutron stars. Magnetars are the subset with exceptionally strong magnetic fields. They have been treated as rare. Rare made it awkward to blame them for the rates of superluminous supernovae, gamma-ray bursts, and fast radio bursts, all of which need a powerful central engine often enough that a scarce magnetar population struggles to keep up.

## One model for objects that used to be filed separately

Earlier tallies tended to treat radio pulsars, magnetars, central compact objects, and X-ray isolated neutron stars as separate boxes. There are evolutionary links between those boxes. A magnetar can spin down, its field can decay, and it can spend part of its life looking like something else. If you ignore the links, you mis-count the birth fraction.

This paper puts the main types of isolated neutron stars into one framework. It folds in how they are distributed in the galaxy, how they spin down, how they cool, how their fields evolve, and the biases of the observations that find them. From that, the authors infer both the magnetar fraction and the supernova rate the Milky Way needs.

The rate part is a check, not a footnote. Core-collapse supernovae from stars of roughly 8 to 25 solar masses are what produce these remnants. To match the neutron stars we actually detect, the models need more than two such explosions per century in the observed population. The team gets a rate two ways: from supernova remnants, and from the neutron-star counts. With that rate in hand, the birth fraction that fits is around 50 percent. Pardo Araujo’s conclusion is that magnetars would then be common enough to power a significant share of those bright transients.

## What “around 50 percent” is allowed to do

It is an average from a model that reproduces galactic observations. Change the field-decay law, or the beaming, or the supernova rate, and the percentage can move. The paper’s claim is that a large fraction is no longer an exotic extra. It is what the unified model prefers. Previous studies that assumed magnetars were rare were using a narrower bookkeeping.

Rea points at the obvious next test: other galaxies. The same synthesis could predict a magnetar population, then compare it with the observed rates of superluminous supernovae, fast radio bursts, and gamma-ray bursts outside the Milky Way. That comparison needs each galaxy’s star-formation history, because the supernova rate will not match ours. Until that is done, the 50 percent is a Milky Way inference.

The Nature Astronomy article is the authority for the model and the fraction. The IEEC note is a clear secondary account. Neither is a catalogue of new magnetars. If you want the observational counterparts, they are still the galactic pulsars and the transient surveys. This paper is about whether those counterparts can be the same objects seen at different ages, born common rather than rare.

### Astronomers caught one of the Universe’s largest structures still being built

- Note URL: https://ojaashampiholi.github.io/the-cosmic-notebook/posts/2026-09-12_cosmology_proto-supercluster-cosmos-z3-1-a/
- Published: 2026-09-12
- Topics: Cosmology & Early Universe
- Freshness context: Published in The Astrophysical Journal on 8 September 2026, within the 15-day freshness window.
- Summary: Astronomers have mapped an enormous young structure called COSMOS-z3.1-A, seen when the Universe was only a few billion years old. It contains many dense groups of galaxies that are still coming together and is the earliest, most distant proto-supercluster yet identified.
- Why it matters: It gives astronomers a rare look at how the Universe built its largest structures from smaller pieces. Instead of seeing a finished supercluster, we are seeing the construction process itself, which helps test our ideas about how gravity shaped the cosmic web over billions of years.
- Suggested next question: Explore the cosmic web and how small groups of galaxies gradually grow into clusters and superclusters.
- Explore further: [NSF NOIRLab: Extremely massive galaxy proto-supercluster smashes distance records](https://noirlab.edu/public/news/noirlab2622/)
- Sources:
  - [NSF NOIRLab](https://noirlab.edu/public/news/noirlab2622/)
  - [Rutgers University](https://newbrunswick.rutgers.edu/news/scientists-see-one-universes-largest-structures-taking-shape)
  - [The Astrophysical Journal](https://doi.org/10.3847/1538-4357/ae8091)

Fuller note:

## A structure with the scaffolding still showing

COSMOS-z3.1-A is a young, enormous gathering of galaxies, mapped when the universe was only a few billion years old. It contains many dense groups that have not finished falling together. NSF NOIRLab’s announcement calls it the earliest, most distant proto-supercluster yet identified. The paper is in The Astrophysical Journal, 8 September 2026, DOI 10.3847/1538-4357/ae8091. Rutgers is the other institutional account attached to this note.

The name carries a redshift. The “z3.1” is the survey’s label for how far back the light started, in the COSMOS field, a patch of sky that has been photographed in nearly every band astronomers use. A proto-supercluster is not a finished supercluster with a single collapsed core. It is the stage before that: groups and clusters already denser than average, still separated, destined to merge if the map has been read right.

“Destined” is the interpretation. The observation is the map: many over-dense groups, at this distance, tied together by their positions and redshifts into one structure rather than a chance alignment on the sky. Chance alignment is the usual skeptic’s alternative for anything huge and far away. A spectroscopic map is how you kill it. The ApJ paper is where that argument has to succeed.

## Why the unfinished version is the useful one

A nearby supercluster is a result. You can weigh it, roughly, and argue about its edges, and you cannot watch it assemble. An early proto-supercluster is the assembly. Gravity is supposed to grow the cosmic web from small lumps into filaments, then into clusters, then into superclusters, over most of the age of the universe. Seeing the intermediate object tests the timetable. If structures this large are already outlined when the universe is only a few billion years old, the seeds and the growth rate have to allow it. If the mass in those groups is later revised down, the record moves.

This note does not add a mass or a galaxy count beyond what the sources given here state. “Many dense groups,” “enormous,” “earliest and most distant yet identified” — those are the claims to keep, and the last one is a record claim that depends on how earlier candidates were defined. Records move when the definition moves. NOIRLab’s wording is the public version of the record. The paper is the version that shows the selection.

## Groups, clusters, superclusters

A group is a handful of galaxies. A cluster is hundreds or thousands, often with a soup of hot gas. A supercluster is a complex of clusters, stretched along the web, not always bound as one object for all future time. “Proto” means the pieces are identified and the mergers are still ahead. COSMOS-z3.1-A is being offered as that middle object, seen early.

The cosmic web is the context, not a second discovery. Galaxies trace filaments of dark matter and gas. Overdense knots on those filaments are where clusters grow. A proto-supercluster is several knots caught in the same large pattern. Mapping one at this distance says the pattern was already in place, which is a statement about initial conditions as much as about the galaxies themselves.

Rutgers’ headline, “one of the universe’s largest structures taking shape,” matches the notebook’s. Taking shape is the right verb. It is not a claim that the supercluster has collapsed, or that every galaxy now inside the map will end in the same cluster. Follow the three sources — NOIRLab, Rutgers, and the ApJ article — if you need the field, the redshifts, and the overdensity cuts. Those cuts are what make “structure” a measurement instead of a picture.

### Tiny worlds beyond Neptune still carry fingerprints from the Solar System’s birth

- Note URL: https://ojaashampiholi.github.io/the-cosmic-notebook/posts/2026-09-11_solar-system_tiny-worlds-beyond-neptune/
- Published: 2026-09-11
- Topics: Solar System & Planetary Science
- Freshness context: Published in The Astronomical Journal and announced by NASA on 8 September 2026, within the 15-day freshness window.
- Summary: Hubble and Webb found 27 previously unknown tiny worlds orbiting beyond Neptune, some among the smallest ever seen directly. Surprisingly, their surfaces resemble those of much larger objects, suggesting these distant leftovers have preserved clues about where and how they formed billions of years ago.
- Why it matters: These icy worlds are leftovers from the era when the planets were being built. Because they appear to have changed less than scientists expected, they may preserve a clearer record of the Solar System’s earliest days and help us reconstruct how the planets, including Earth, came together.
- Suggested next question: Explore the Kuiper Belt and why objects beyond Neptune act like a frozen archaeological record of the early Solar System.
- Explore further: [NASA: Hubble, Webb Find Far-out Solar System Objects ‘Remember’ Past](https://science.nasa.gov/missions/hubble/nasas-hubble-webb-find-far-out-solar-system-objects-remember-past/)
- Sources:
  - [NASA Science](https://science.nasa.gov/missions/hubble/nasas-hubble-webb-find-far-out-solar-system-objects-remember-past/)
  - [NASA Scientific Visualization Studio](https://svs.gsfc.nasa.gov/15092)

Fuller note:

## Twenty-seven points of light, smaller than the survey expected

Hubble and Webb, used together, found 27 previously unknown worlds beyond Neptune. Some are among the smallest ever seen directly. The smallest diameter in NASA’s account is about 5 kilometres, roughly 3 miles, about five times smaller than sensitive ground-based surveys can pick out. One of them is as faint, NASA says, as a swarm of fireflies on the Moon seen from Earth. Two papers in The Astronomical Journal, out with NASA’s 8 September 2026 announcement, cover color and composition on one side and the size distribution on the other.

These are trans-Neptunian objects, TNOs. They orbit outside Neptune. Most of the population is more than 100 million times dimmer than a star you can see by eye. Beyond Neptune, the disk of dust and pebbles built city-sized planetesimals and then stopped. The later mergers that made planets did not finish out there. What remains is a cold archive of the building blocks.

The teams were led by PhD candidates at the University of Victoria, with the National Research Council of Canada, and at Northern Arizona University. Anastasia Morgan at NAU led the color and composition study. Marielle Eduardo at Victoria led the sizes. David Trilling at NAU is a co-author. Hubble took the visible light. Webb took the infrared. Color, in this game, is a rough fingerprint of the surface ices and reddening material. Orbits tell you which dynamical family an object belongs to.

## They still look like the big ones

The prior expectation was that small TNOs would be battered. Collisions should have refreshed or altered their surfaces, so the tiniest bodies ought to have different colors from Pluto-scale objects. They do not. The small ones follow the same color relations as the larger family members.

There are two dynamical families in the sample. “Cold” TNOs are on rounder orbits in the plane, thought to be near where they formed. “Hot” TNOs are on tilted, stretched orbits. They are thought to have formed between Uranus and Neptune and been scattered outward when the giant planets migrated. Both families kept the colors of their birthplaces. Trilling’s point is that the hot ones still carry a signature of where they formed, after the orbits were scrambled. Morgan’s is that the smallest objects are “remembering” the formation history that collisions were supposed to erase.

Eduardo’s size result is the other surprise. The distribution of sizes is similar for the hot and the cold populations, even though they formed in different parts of the disk. And there are fewer very small bodies than some planet-formation models predicted. Webb is what reached those sizes. The shortage is relative to the models, not a claim that the belt is empty.

## Two readings, both still open

The color match can mean collisions are rarer than expected, or that collisions happen and the surface composition survives them anyway. The teams have not separated those.
