The similar size distributions can mean planetesimal formation does not care much whether the disk was hot or cold, dense or fluffy. That is Eduardo’s suggestion, and it is a suggestion about a process, drawn from one deep patch of sky.

This is not a full census of the Kuiper belt. It is the deepest look so far at the faint end, in one field, with two telescopes that see different wavelengths. NASA’s Scientific Visualization Studio piece is the visual companion to the science release. The Astronomical Journal papers are the authority for the photometry and the size function.

The archaeological value is real and limited. These leftovers changed less than the collision story predicted, so their surfaces are a cleaner record of the disk than a heavily reprocessed population would be. Cleaner is not complete. Orbits were scrambled for the hot family. Sizes may have been. The ice chemistry is what seems to have held.

### Astronomers found a hidden class of some of the most energetic objects in galaxies

- Note URL: https://ojaashampiholi.github.io/the-cosmic-notebook/posts/2026-09-10_stars-stellar-evolution_chandra-hypersoft-sources/
- Published: 2026-09-10
- Topics: Stars & Stellar Evolution
- Freshness context: Published in Nature Astronomy on 9 September 2026, within the 15-day freshness window.
- Summary: Astronomers searching old observations from NASA’s Chandra X-ray Observatory found 84 objects in six galaxies that had largely escaped notice because most of their energy comes out in a difficult-to-observe form of ultraviolet light. Scientists do not yet know exactly what they are, but they may be systems where a dense stellar remnant — such as a white dwarf, neutron star or black hole — is pulling material from a companion star.
- Why it matters: These objects may fill in a missing part of our picture of how stars live and die. Some could be systems on the way to becoming Type Ia supernovae — stellar explosions that astronomers use to measure the expansion of the Universe — while their intense ultraviolet light may also help explain how gas between stars is energized inside galaxies.
- Suggested next question: Explore how a white dwarf can pull material from a companion star and eventually trigger a Type Ia supernova.
- Explore further: [Nature Astronomy: Hypersoft X-ray sources as a low-energy class of luminous cosmic emitter](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41550-026-02959-7)
- Sources:
  - [Nature Astronomy](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41550-026-02959-7)
  - [NASA Chandra X-ray Observatory](https://science.nasa.gov/missions/chandra/nasas-chandra-unveils-mysterious-x-ray-objects/)

Fuller note:

## Eighty-four objects that were easy to miss

A search through old observations from NASA’s Chandra X-ray Observatory turned up 84 objects in six galaxies. They had been easy to skip because most of their energy comes out as ultraviolet light, in a band that is miserable to observe, rather than as the X-rays Chandra is famous for catching. The Nature Astronomy paper, published on 9 September 2026, calls the class hypersoft X-ray sources: a low-energy end of the luminous compact emitters. NASA’s Chandra write-up is the other account in this note.

“Hypersoft” is a spectrum word. Soft X-rays are the lower-energy ones. These sources are softer still, piled up at the edge of what an X-ray telescope records, with the bulk of the power in the extreme ultraviolet. If your pipeline is tuned for harder sources, you under-count them. That is a selection effect, and it is why a hidden class can sit in an archive.

## The identity is not known

The paper does not say what they are. The working idea, reported as a possibility, is a dense stellar remnant pulling material off a companion: a white dwarf, a neutron star, or a black hole, with a disk or a stream that radiates at these low energies. Accretion makes soft spectra when the inner flow is not extremely hot, or when the viewing angle and the absorption cooperate. Several kinds of remnant can do that. The spectra in hand do not yet sort them.

Two consequences are why the class is worth a note, and both are conditional.

Some of the white-dwarf versions could be on the way to a Type Ia supernova. A white dwarf that gains mass from a companion can approach the mass where it detonates. Those explosions are the standard candles used to measure cosmic expansion. A missing population of the systems that precede them is a missing part of the candle factory. “Could be” is not a count of how many of the 84 will explode, or when.

The ultraviolet light is the other consequence. Extreme UV ionizes gas between stars. If a galaxy contains more of these sources than the X-ray catalogues suggested, the energy budget of that gas changes. Again: a plausible role, not a measured fraction of the ionizing field.

## What to hold onto

Hold onto 84 sources, six galaxies, an archival search, a spectrum that peaks in a hard-to-see ultraviolet band, and an open identification. Let go of any sentence that names a single remnant as the answer. Chandra can find the soft X-ray tail. It cannot, from these data alone, weigh the compact object or watch the companion.

NASA’s write-up is clear that the objects had largely escaped notice. That is the observational point. The stellar-evolution point is the possible place they occupy between ordinary binaries and the explosions or the ionized gas astronomers already study. Filling a gap in a sequence is useful even while the objects at the gap stay unclassified.

The Nature Astronomy article is the authority for the sample and the spectra. Until a follow-up pins the compact-object mass, or catches a supernova in one of these galaxies and ties it back, the remnant story stays a candidate list: white dwarf, neutron star, black hole, each with a companion, each still allowed.

### Mysterious cosmic flashes can reveal where the Universe hides its ordinary matter

- Note URL: https://ojaashampiholi.github.io/the-cosmic-notebook/posts/2026-09-09_cosmology_fast-radio-bursts-hidden-matter/
- Published: 2026-09-09
- Topics: Cosmology & Early Universe
- Freshness context: Published in Nature Astronomy on 8 September 2026, within the 15-day freshness window.
- Summary: Fast radio bursts are extremely brief flashes of radio waves from distant galaxies. As their signals travel toward Earth, the ordinary matter between galaxies subtly changes them, letting astronomers use the flashes like backlights to trace otherwise hard-to-see material spread through the Universe.
- Why it matters: Most of the Universe’s ordinary matter is difficult to see directly because it is spread thinly through space. This study shows that fast radio bursts can help map that hidden material and reveal how galaxies push it around, making it easier to separate the effects of ordinary matter from deeper mysteries such as dark matter and dark energy.
- Suggested next question: Explore the cosmic web: the enormous network of galaxies, gas and matter that gives the Universe its large-scale structure.
- Explore further: [Nature Astronomy: Signatures of suppressed matter clustering revealed by fast radio bursts](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41550-026-02957-9)
- Sources:
  - [Nature Astronomy](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41550-026-02957-9)
  - [Caltech](https://www.caltech.edu/about/news/fast-radio-bursts-poised-to-help-with-biggest-cosmic-mysteries)

Fuller note:

## A flash, then a fog

Fast radio bursts last milliseconds. They arrive from other galaxies, and on the way they cross gas that is too thin to see easily. That gas slows lower radio frequencies more than higher ones. The delay is a dispersion measure: a count of the electrons along the path. More electrons, more delay. A burst becomes a backlight.

A Nature Astronomy paper published on 8 September 2026, “Signatures of suppressed matter clustering revealed by fast radio bursts,” uses a sample of about 100 of these bursts to measure how clumpy ordinary matter is on the large scales around and between galaxies. Kritti Sharma, a graduate student at Caltech working with Vikram Ravi, led the study. Elisabeth Krause at the University of Arizona is a co-author. Caltech’s news piece is the secondary source.

Ordinary matter here means baryons: protons, neutrons, the stuff of gas and stars and people. A large share of it is not in galaxies. It is spread through the cosmic web, and through the halos just outside galaxies, where it is ionized and faint. Dispersion does not care that it is faint. Electrons are electrons.

## The measurement is a smoothing, smaller than the X-ray one

Galaxies push this gas around. Central black holes blow winds. Supernovae dump energy. The process is called feedback, and it moves gas outward, which makes the matter distribution smoother. Smoother matter looks, in a cosmological analysis, a lot like the signature of massive neutrinos, or like some versions of dark energy and dark matter. If you cannot measure the feedback piece on its own, you cannot tell those effects apart. Ravi’s group is blunt about that resemblance.

What this sample shows: feedback does smooth the gas, and it does so less than earlier measurements from the eROSITA X-ray telescope and from the Atacama Cosmology Telescope. That “less” is the result. It is the first time FRBs have been used to measure the feedback impact on clumping directly, in the regions around and between galaxies. Krause’s comparison is that the constraint is already competitive with those X-ray and microwave surveys, from only about 100 bursts.

The bursts’ own engines are a separate uncertainty. Magnetars — neutron stars with extreme magnetic fields — are a leading guess, not a settled identification for every burst. You do not need the engine to use the delay. You need the distance, the frequency sweep, and a model of what else is in the way, including the Milky Way’s own electrons. Those subtractions are where the measurement can go wrong, and they are why the paper, not this note, is the authority.

## What this does not yet settle

Dark energy, dark matter, and the neutrino mass are not measured here. They are the reason the smoothing matters. Sky surveys map clumping in order to get at those three. Feedback imitates them. An independent FRB number lets the surveys subtract a better feedback term. Sharma’s line is that these data can sharpen the cosmology experiments. That is a use, not a completed answer.

The sample is small next to what is coming. Caltech’s Deep Synoptic Array, planned for a remote valley in Nevada by 2029 and funded by Schmidt Sciences, is expected to find tens of thousands of bursts. Ravi, a co-principal investigator, expects that catalogue to sit alongside Euclid, DESI, Rubin, and the Roman telescope. Those are plans. The Nature Astronomy result is the hundred-burst measurement.

One practical distinction, if you only remember one: dispersion traces electrons, which trace ionized ordinary matter. It does not see dark matter. Its power is that it stops dark matter and dark energy analyses from quietly absorbing a baryon effect they did not measure.

### Two massive baby stars may have become a binary after forming separately

- Note URL: https://ojaashampiholi.github.io/the-cosmic-notebook/posts/2026-09-08_stars-stellar-evolution_massive-binary-capture/
- Published: 2026-09-08
- Topics: Stars & Stellar Evolution
- Freshness context: Published in Nature Astronomy on 7 September 2026, within the 15-day freshness window.
- Summary: Astronomers followed two massive baby stars and found that their stretched orbit and tilted surrounding disks are hard to explain if the stars were born together. The evidence instead suggests they formed separately, passed close to one another, and became gravitationally bound as a pair.
- Why it matters: Most massive stars live with a stellar companion, but scientists still do not fully understand how those partnerships begin. This result suggests that some massive binary stars may form through a later gravitational encounter, adding a new route to the story of how the biggest stars are born and evolve.
- Suggested next question: Explore why massive stars are so often found in binary systems and how a companion can change the way a star lives and dies.
- Explore further: [Nature Astronomy: An eccentric massive protobinary assembled via a core-merger parabolic encounter](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41550-026-02953-z)
- Sources:
  - [Nature Astronomy](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41550-026-02953-z)
  - [ALMA Observatory](https://alma-telescope.jp/news/mbassemble-202609.html)

Fuller note:

## The orbit does not look like a shared birth

Most massive stars have a companion. How the pair got that way is less settled. They might have collapsed out of the same core, already bound. Or they might have formed apart and been captured later. A Nature Astronomy paper published on 7 September 2026 argues for the second route in one specific system: two massive baby stars whose stretched orbit and tilted disks are hard to produce if they formed together.

The title of the paper says the quiet part aloud. “An eccentric massive protobinary assembled via a core-merger parabolic encounter.” Eccentric means the orbit is elongated, not a tidy circle. A parabolic encounter is a close pass on a trajectory that is just barely unbound, the kind of flyby that can end in capture if the pair loses a little energy during the meeting. “Core-merger” points at the dense star-forming cores ALMA can resolve. The ALMA Observatory’s note on the result is the other source attached to this notebook entry.

Baby, here, means the stars are still forming. They are massive, still gathering, and each is wrapped in a disk. Those disks are tilted relative to each other and relative to the orbit. Disks that grew inside one shared, rotating core tend to remember the same angular-momentum direction. A later capture does not have to be so polite. The two spins can meet at an angle.

## What was hard to explain, and what the team prefers

The observation is the geometry: a stretched orbit, misaligned disks, two massive protostars. The interpretation is the history. Separate formation, a close pass, then a bound pair. The paper is saying the together-from-birth model has trouble with that geometry, and the encounter model has less trouble. That is a comparative fit, not a film of the flyby. Nobody watched the capture.

Capture of this kind matters because the companion changes everything that follows. Massive stars in pairs exchange mass, spin each other up, and often die in ways a single star does not. A later capture is a different clock from a birth binary. The two stars can be at different stages when they meet. Their disks can be truncated or tilted by the encounter itself, which then changes how planets or further companions could form, if any do. The note does not claim planets. It claims a route into the binary.

## One system is a route, not a fraction

Nothing here says most massive binaries formed this way. It says at least this one is difficult to file under co-formation, and that a parabolic encounter can assemble a massive protobinary. Population numbers would need a survey. ALMA can do the geometry for the nearest, brightest cores. It cannot yet hand over a rate.

If you want the mechanism in one picture: two cores, two disks, a pass close enough that gravity binds them, an orbit left eccentric because the capture was recent and the orbit has not been rounded out. Tidal forces and leftover gas may circularize it later. The eccentricity is a clue that “later” has not finished.

Read the Nature Astronomy article for the orbit fit and the disk angles. Read the ALMA note for the observatory’s version of the same observation. The next question in the notebook — why massive stars are so often paired, and what a companion does to the death — is larger than this one system, and this system is one concrete way the pairing can start after the births.

### Comets may be carrying water into a young planet-forming system

- Note URL: https://ojaashampiholi.github.io/the-cosmic-notebook/posts/2026-09-07_planet-formation_pds70-exocomets-water/
- Published: 2026-09-07
- Topics: Planet Formation
- Freshness context: Published in Nature Communications on 24 August 2026, within the 15-day freshness window.
- Summary: Astronomers found signs of comets moving through the young PDS 70 system, where planets are still forming. Computer simulations show that giant planets there could fling icy bodies inward, possibly carrying water from the cold outer system toward the region where rocky planets can grow.
- Why it matters: Earth’s water had to come from somewhere, and scientists are still working out how much arrived on comets or asteroids. Seeing a similar possible delivery route in another young planetary system suggests that moving icy bodies may be one natural way growing planets receive water, although more observations are needed to confirm the comets directly.
- Suggested next question: Explore how comets and asteroids may have delivered water to the early Earth.
- Explore further: [Nature Communications: Potential sublimating exocomets around the young star PDS 70](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41467-026-76880-y)
- Sources:
  - [Nature Communications](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41467-026-76880-y)
  - [Lund University](https://www.lunduniversity.lu.se/article/comets-may-have-transported-water-young-planetary-system)

Fuller note:

## A young system with planets already in it, and a hint of ice on the move

PDS 70 is one of the few young stars where planets have been seen still inside the disk. A Nature Communications paper published on 24 August 2026 reports signs of comets moving through that system. The signs are not a photograph of a nucleus. They are the spectral and dynamical evidence the team presents for bodies that are sublimating — ice turning to gas as the bodies warm.

The second half of the result is a simulation, and it should stay in a separate column. Giant planets in PDS 70 can scatter icy bodies inward. Those bodies can carry water from the cold outer disk toward the zone where rocky planets can grow. Lund University’s account of the work puts the transportation idea in the headline. The paper’s own title is narrower: potential sublimating exocomets around the young star PDS 70. “Potential” is in the title for a reason.

## What would count as a comet here

An exocomet is a comet in another planetary system. You almost never see the rock. You see gas that appears and disappears, or absorption lines that move, as a small icy body swings close to the star and vents. In a disk that still holds planets, those vents are easy to confuse with disk winds, with accretion funnels, and with the planets’ own wakes. The paper is arguing that the signatures fit comets better than those alternatives. That argument is the result to read carefully, not a headcount of confirmed nuclei.

Earth’s water is the reason anyone outside planet-formation circles cares. The oceans had to arrive or be made. Comets and asteroids are the usual couriers in our own system, and the fractions are still argued. PDS 70 does not settle Earth’s ledger. It shows a route that can operate while planets and the disk still share the same system: a giant planet as a gravitational sling, icy leftovers as the cargo, the inner disk as the destination.

## Simulation is not the same sentence as the detection

Keep the two claims apart. The observational claim is that there are signs of comets in PDS 70. The dynamical claim is that the known giant planets are capable of flinging icy bodies inward, and that water could move with them. A simulation that shows a path is evidence the path is open. It is not a measurement of how much water arrived, or of how often the scattering happens.

More observations are what would promote the comets from “signs” to objects with orbits. Repeated spectra, a periodicity, a composition that matches ice rather than disk gas: those are the sorts of checks that close the gap. Until then, the careful sentence in the notebook’s summary stands. A delivery route like the one proposed for early Earth appears available in a system that is still being built. Availability is not delivery.

Nature Communications is the authority for the signatures. Lund’s article is the secondary explanation. Neither should be stretched into a statement that PDS 70’s rocky planets, if it has them, already have oceans. The star is young. The experiment is still running.

### Scientists may have seen a particle of dark matter — but they aren't sure yet

- Note URL: https://ojaashampiholi.github.io/the-cosmic-notebook/posts/2026-09-06_fundamental-physics_lz-dark-matter-candidate/
- Published: 2026-09-06
- Topics: Gravity & Fundamental Physics
- Freshness context: 15-day window — LUX-ZEPLIN announced the result on 1 September 2026.
- Summary: An underground experiment built to search for dark matter recorded one unusual event that looks like something a dark-matter particle could have caused. But a single event is not enough to rule out coincidence or another explanation, so scientists are treating it as an intriguing clue rather than a discovery.
- Why it matters: We know dark matter exists because we can see its gravity affecting galaxies, but nobody has directly identified what it is made of. If future observations find more events like this and other explanations can be ruled out, scientists could finally get a direct clue about the particles that make up much of the universe's unseen matter.
- Suggested next question: Explore how scientists know dark matter exists even though they still do not know what it is made of.
- Explore further: [LUX-ZEPLIN: new high-energy dark-matter search result](https://lz.lbl.gov/)
- Sources:
  - [LUX-ZEPLIN Collaboration](https://lz.lbl.gov/)
  - [Berkeley Lab](https://newscenter.lbl.gov/2026/09/01/lz-sees-surprising-result-in-search-for-dark-matter/)
  - [Reuters](https://www.reuters.com/science/scientists-make-potential-breakthrough-search-dark-matter-2026-09-01/)

Fuller note:

## One event, and a refusal to call it a discovery

LUX-ZEPLIN recorded a single particle interaction that is hard to explain with the backgrounds the collaboration knows how to model. It sits in the region of the data where a dark-matter particle could show up, and where ordinary backgrounds are supposed to be scarce. The collaboration is not calling it a detection.

Rick Gaitskell, a professor at Brown and LZ’s spokesperson, said as much when the result was presented: they are intrigued, they do not want to get ahead of one event, and they are not claiming to have seen dark matter. The analysis was shown at the 2026 TeV Particle Astrophysics conference in Japan. A paper is headed for arXiv and Physical Review Letters. Berkeley Lab’s 1 September 2026 write-up is the account used here, with the collaboration’s own site.

LZ sits nearly a mile underground at the Sanford Underground Research Facility in South Dakota. Berkeley Lab manages it. About 250 scientists and engineers from 39 institutions work on it. The detector holds 10 tonnes of ultrapure liquid xenon and is built to look for WIMPs, weakly interacting massive particles, one of the long-standing guesses for what dark matter might be. Dark matter is still a gravitational fact — it outweighs ordinary matter, about 85 percent of the mass — and an unidentified substance. Nobody has a confirmed particle.

## What the new search actually did

The collaboration had already looked at 220 live days of data, March 2023 through April 2024, for the simplest kind of WIMP scatter, the faint ones. This analysis opened a different slice of that same dataset: interactions that could deposit more energy. Sam Eriksen of the University of Bristol, lead author, says they spent months on backgrounds in a region they had not explored in this exposure. LZ expects real dark-matter events to be extremely rare. A handful could be a first detection. One is a hint.

If this event were a WIMP, the collaboration’s reading is that its mass would likely be at least 200 GeV/c², more than 200 times a proton, and that the interaction would be a less simple kind than the baseline model. That “if” is the interpretation. The fact is one outlier that survived the checks they know how to run.

The statistical weight is 2.6 sigma. In this analysis that corresponds to about a 0.5 percent chance the event is a known background. Five sigma is the usual discovery line in this field. 2.6 is not close. Aaron Manalaysay at Berkeley Lab, chair of LZ’s Institutional Board, calls it the first outlier in his experiments that still looks valid after you stare at it, and he is explicit that a rare background they have not thought of remains on the table.

## Why the underground lab is part of the result

A xenon tank records flashes when something deposits energy. Cosmic rays, neutrons from the rock, and radioactive traces in the materials all do that too. The mile of rock cuts the cosmic rays. A water tank and outer detectors tag neutrons. Software then throws out events that look like the mimics. The remaining search region is quiet enough that a single leftover event is news. It is not quiet enough, with this exposure, to decide what the event was.

LZ is still running, and it already holds the largest dark-matter dataset of this kind. More days will either grow this hint or wash it out. Until more events land in the same place, the honest sentence is Gaitskell’s. Something in the box is interesting. Dark matter has not been identified.

Reuters reported the announcement the same day as Berkeley Lab. Neither replaces the paper. When the Physical Review Letters article is public, it supersedes this note on the energy, the cuts, and the background model.

### The universe is making fewer stars — but it hasn’t run out of hydrogen

- Note URL: https://ojaashampiholi.github.io/the-cosmic-notebook/posts/2026-09-05_galaxy-evolution_star-formation-hydrogen/
- Published: 2026-09-05
- Topics: Galaxies & Galactic Evolution
- Freshness context: Published in Nature Astronomy on 1 September 2026, within the 15-day freshness window.
- Summary: Using China’s FAST radio telescope together with DESI data for about 2.5 million galaxies, astronomers found that cosmic star formation has fallen by roughly a factor of 2.46 over the past 4.5 billion years, while the universe’s neutral atomic hydrogen reservoir has declined far less. The result suggests the problem is not simply that galaxies have run out of raw gas, but that they have become less efficient at turning atomic hydrogen into the denser molecular gas that actually forms stars.
- Why it matters: For years, one simple explanation for the universe’s fading star formation was that galaxies were gradually using up their fuel. This study weakens that explanation: plenty of neutral hydrogen remains, so astronomers now have to focus more on how gas flows through galaxies and why the conversion from atomic to molecular gas has become less effective.
- Suggested next question: Explore the difference between atomic hydrogen and molecular hydrogen, and why stars form mainly from the latter.
- Explore further: [Nature Astronomy: Weak evolution of cosmic atomic hydrogen over the past 4.5 billion years](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41550-026-02965-9)
- Sources:
  - [Nature Astronomy](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41550-026-02965-9)
  - [Chinese Academy of Sciences / EurekAlert](https://e3.eurekalert.org/news-releases/1142061)

Fuller note:

## The fuel is still there. The factory slowed.

Cosmic star formation has dropped by roughly a factor of 2.46 over the past 4.5 billion years. Over that same stretch, the universe’s reservoir of neutral atomic hydrogen has declined far less. That pairing is the result in a Nature Astronomy paper published on 1 September 2026. The observations use China’s FAST radio telescope together with DESI data for about 2.5 million galaxies.

Stars form from molecular hydrogen, H2, the two-atom version, inside cold dense clouds. The atom-only gas, H I, is the larger tank. It has to cool, gather, and become molecular before it becomes a star. A galaxy can be rich in H I and still be a poor star factory if that conversion is sluggish.

For years the simple story of the universe’s fading starlight was depletion. Galaxies used up the tank. A drop in star formation of more than a factor of two, beside a much smaller drop in atomic hydrogen, is awkward for that story. The gas is not gone in proportion to the stars that stopped forming.

## What the ratio is allowed to mean

The paper’s reading, and the reading this notebook should keep, is about efficiency. Galaxies have become worse at turning atomic hydrogen into the denser molecular gas that actually forms stars. That is an interpretation of the two trends. It is a strong one, because the alternative (the tank ran dry) does not match the hydrogen measurement. It is still an interpretation: the survey does not hand you a molecule-by-molecule account of every disk. It hands you a cosmic average.

FAST is what makes the hydrogen side possible. The 21-centimetre line from neutral hydrogen is faint, and you need a huge collecting area plus a huge galaxy sample if you want the average over billions of years rather than a portrait of one nearby spiral. DESI supplies the galaxies: distances, so the hydrogen can be placed in time. About 2.5 million of them is the sample size attached to this result. The Chinese Academy of Sciences summary, carried by EurekAlert, is the institutional account alongside the paper.

## Where the gas can stall

Between atomic hydrogen and a star there are several stalls. The gas has to reach the disk. It has to cool. It has to form H2 on dust grains. It has to collapse past its own turbulence and past whatever the galaxy is doing to stir it. Feedback from earlier stars, a bar, a hot halo, a black hole: any of those can change the conversion without deleting the H I. The Andromeda note in this notebook is about one galaxy’s turbulence. This one is the cosmic average of the outcome.

The number 2.46 should stay attached to star formation, not be casually reapplied to the gas. The gas decline is “far less,” which is the paper’s comparison, not a second precise factor I am going to invent. Someone reading the Nature Astronomy article (DOI 10.1038/s41550-026-02965-9) should treat that article as the source of both curves.

The next distinction is worth making before the next paper: atomic hydrogen is the reservoir you see in the radio; molecular hydrogen is the fuel in the clouds. Stars form from the second. A universe that still has plenty of the first can look quiet anyway.

### Hubble catches a giant 10-sided wave forming around Saturn’s south pole

- Note URL: https://ojaashampiholi.github.io/the-cosmic-notebook/posts/2026-09-04_solar-system_saturn-south-pole-decagon/
- Published: 2026-09-04
- Topics: Solar System & Planetary Science
- Freshness context: Published in Science Advances on 2 September 2026, within the 15-day freshness window.
- Summary: Hubble and ground-based observations have revealed a giant decagonal atmospheric wave around Saturn’s south pole, the first large regular-sided jet pattern ever seen in the planet’s southern hemisphere. Faint signs appear in data from 2023 and 2024, while the structure became much clearer in 2025, suggesting astronomers may be watching a huge planetary weather pattern develop in real time.
- Why it matters: Saturn’s famous north-polar hexagon has persisted for decades, but this newly emerging southern decagon appears younger and more dynamic. Following it as it evolves could help scientists understand how giant atmospheric waves form, why Saturn produces polygon-shaped jet patterns, and whether such structures can become long-lived.
- Suggested next question: Explore Saturn’s north-polar hexagon and why a jet stream can organize into a stable geometric wave instead of a simple circular band.
- Explore further: [Science Advances: A decagon wave around Saturn’s south pole](https://doi.org/10.1126/sciadv.aee4251)
- Sources:
  - [Science Advances](https://doi.org/10.1126/sciadv.aee4251)
  - [NASA Hubble](https://science.nasa.gov/missions/hubble/nasas-hubble-tracks-new-decagon-encircling-saturns-south-pole/)
  - [University of Leicester](https://le.ac.uk/news/2026/august/observations-mysterious-shape-saturn-clouds)

Fuller note:

## A ten-sided wave, still settling in

Hubble has caught a giant decagonal wave around Saturn’s south pole. It is the first large, regular-sided jet pattern seen in the planet’s southern hemisphere. Faint signs are in data from 2023 and 2024. By 2025 the shape was much clearer. The paper is in Science Advances, 2 September 2026.

That timeline is the interesting part. Saturn’s north-polar hexagon has been there every time observers have looked, for more than 40 years. Amy Simon, co-author and principal investigator of Hubble’s Outer Planet Atmospheres Legacy program at NASA Goddard, says this southern feature is different: it appears to be strengthening. The OPAL program has photographed the outer planets once a year for more than a decade, which is why a slow pattern can be caught in the act instead of as a single postcard.

The south pole has also been hard to see. Saturn’s seasons tipped it back into view from Earth. Ground-based observers found it first. Agustín Sánchez-Lavega, at the University of the Basque Country, leads the study. He and amateur astronomers Trevor Barry and Jean-Paul Oger noticed a subtle undulating band in 2024 images contributed to the Planetary Virtual Observatory Laboratory. 2025 ground images pushed harder toward a ten-sided shape. Hubble then confirmed the feature was already present in 2023.

## Not a cloud doodle

The wave sits in one of Saturn’s jet streams and extends through several layers of the atmosphere. Different Hubble filters look at different altitudes, and the apparent position of the decagon shifts slightly between them. That shift is evidence the structure is vertically extended, not a stain on the cloud tops.

Sánchez-Lavega’s group had been looking for a southern twin of the hexagon in Hubble images since 1990, because the north-south jet system is roughly symmetric. Cassini, in orbit from 2004 to 2017, showed no long-lived southern polygon. So this is new on a planet we have watched closely. Simon’s question is the right one: why did it form now?

## What is measured, and what is still open

Measured: a ten-sided wave, multi-layered, emerging over 2023–2025, first large regular polygon in the south. Interpreted, not yet shown: that it will last for decades the way the hexagon has, or that the same fluid mechanics produced both shapes. The authors want more Hubble time, JWST, and computer models before they will say how it formed, how long it may last, or how it compares with the north.

A jet can prefer a polygon over a circle when the wind’s speed changes sharply with latitude and the waves that fit inside that shear lock into a standing pattern. The hexagon is the textbook case. A decagon would be a different number of sides in a different jet, possibly a younger one. Copying the hexagon’s explanation onto the south pole is the temptation. The data so far only justify the geometry and the fact that it is growing.

Mike Wong, a co-author at UC Berkeley, notes that OPAL’s finds tend to come from the stack of years, not from one visit. This decagon is that kind of find. Science Advances (DOI 10.1126/sciadv.aee4251) carries the analysis. NASA’s Hubble write-up and the University of Leicester’s note are the institutional accounts. The next useful comparison is the northern hexagon itself: a jet that chose a shape and then kept it, which this southern wave has not yet had time to do.

### JWST finds hidden low-mass stars that may make early massive galaxies up to four times heavier

- Note URL: https://ojaashampiholi.github.io/the-cosmic-notebook/posts/2026-09-03_galaxy-evolution_hidden-mass-early-galaxies/
- Published: 2026-09-03
- Topics: Galaxies & Galactic Evolution; Stars & Stellar Evolution
- Freshness context: Published in Nature Astronomy on 21 August 2026, within the 15-day freshness window.
- Summary: Using JWST spectra of nine massive, quiescent galaxies, astronomers found evidence that the most massive systems contain many more faint, low-mass stars than standard assumptions predict. If similar stellar populations were already present in their earlier ancestors, some of JWST’s surprisingly mature early galaxies could be about four times more massive than current estimates suggest, making their rapid formation even harder to explain.
- Why it matters: Astronomers estimate distant galaxy masses by assuming a typical mix of stellar masses, but this result suggests that assumption may fail for the biggest systems. If so, models of how galaxies assembled so much stellar mass so early in cosmic history face an even tougher challenge.
- Suggested next question: Explore the initial mass function: the distribution of stellar birth masses that astronomers use to convert a galaxy’s light into an estimate of its total stellar mass.
- Explore further: [Nature Astronomy: Hidden mass in early galaxies revealed by bottom-heavy initial mass functions](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41550-026-02932-4)
- Sources:
  - [Nature Astronomy](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41550-026-02932-4)
  - [Penn State](https://pure.psu.edu/en/publications/hidden-mass-in-early-galaxies-revealed-by-bottom-heavy-initial-ma/)

Fuller note:

## Light is not mass

A galaxy’s stellar mass is usually inferred, not weighed. You see light. You assume a mix of bright stars and faint ones, then scale up. That mix is the initial mass function: how many stars are born at each mass. High-mass stars dominate the light and die young. Low-mass stars dominate the mass and linger. If the mix is bottom-heavy, with more faint stars than the standard assumption, the same glow hides more mass.

A Nature Astronomy paper published on 21 August 2026 applies that worry to nine massive, quiescent galaxies observed with JWST. Quiescent means they have largely stopped forming stars. They are not the dusty, frantic systems that are easiest to misread. The team reports evidence that the most massive of these systems contain many more faint, low-mass stars than the usual recipe predicts.

That is the measurement claim, as the notebook has it from the paper: the stellar populations look bottom-heavy. The Penn State record of the same work carries the title “Hidden mass in early galaxies revealed by bottom-heavy initial mass functions.”

## The factor of four is a conditional

The excerpt’s striking number is not “these nine galaxies are four times heavier than we thought,” full stop. It is conditional. If similar populations were already present in their earlier ancestors, some of JWST’s surprisingly mature early galaxies could be about four times more massive than current estimates. “Could” is doing real work. The spectra are of quiescent systems. The early, still-forming galaxies are a different set. Carrying the result backward is an inference.

If the inference holds, the formation problem gets worse, not better. JWST has been finding galaxies that look heavy very early. Adding hidden low-mass stars would raise the mass that had to be assembled in a short time. Models that were already strained would be more strained. That is why the result matters even though nine galaxies is not a census of the early universe.

## Where the assumption usually hides

The standard conversion from light to mass is good enough for a lot of nearby galaxies, which is why it became the default. It fails quietly. Two galaxies with the same brightness can differ in mass if one is full of red dwarfs and the other is not. Star-formation histories, chemical patterns, and the light from the giants all get folded into the fit. JWST’s spectra of these quiescent systems are what let the authors ask the question directly instead of adopting the Milky Way’s mix and moving on.

Nothing in the note says every early galaxy is bottom-heavy. The claim is aimed at the most massive quiescent ones, and then, more tentatively, at their ancestors. A bottom-heavy function also changes how much mass you assign to the stars you cannot see, which changes how much room is left for gas and dark matter inside the same dynamical measurement, if you have one. This paper’s route is stellar populations, not dynamics.

Treat the Nature Astronomy paper, DOI 10.1038/s41550-026-02932-4, as the authority for the spectral fits. The factor-of-four statement belongs in the conditional column until someone measures those ancestor galaxies the same way. The useful next step is the initial mass function itself: not as a slogan, but as the table of birth masses that turns a spectrum into a mass. Change the table, and a generation of early-galaxy masses moves with it.

### JWST shows planet formation is a race against disappearing gas

- Note URL: https://ojaashampiholi.github.io/the-cosmic-notebook/posts/2026-09-02_planet-formation_jwst-disk-winds/
- Published: 2026-09-02
- Topics: Planet Formation
- Freshness context: Published online in The Astronomical Journal on 25 August 2026, within the 15-day freshness window.
- Summary: Using archival observations from JWST's Mid-Infrared Instrument, astronomers studied 72 young, mostly Sun-like stars to see how gas escapes from their planet-forming disks. They found that early, actively accreting systems are dominated by magnetically driven jets and molecular-plus-atomic winds, while older, lower-accretion systems increasingly show mainly atomic winds, including photoevaporative flows heated by stellar radiation. Extended gas emission was detected in 66 of the 72 disks, including conical molecular-hydrogen winds in 46 systems and fast neon jets in 40. Together, the sample turns individual snapshots into an evolutionary sequence and shows that the raw gas needed to build giant planets is being steadily removed as planetary systems mature.
- Why it matters: Giant planets such as Jupiter need large amounts of gas, but that reservoir does not remain available indefinitely. By showing how the dominant gas-loss mechanisms change with age across dozens of systems, this study gives astronomers a clearer physical clock for planet formation and helps constrain when gas giants must assemble their atmospheres before the disk is dispersed.
- Suggested next question: Explore photoevaporation: how ultraviolet and X-ray radiation from a young star can heat a protoplanetary disk until its gas escapes into space.
- Explore further: [SETI Institute: JWST Reveals a Race Against Time for Forming Planets](https://www.seti.org/news/jwst-reveals-a-race-against-time/)
- Sources:
  - [SETI Institute](https://www.seti.org/news/jwst-reveals-a-race-against-time/)
  - [The Astronomical Journal / DOI](https://doi.org/10.3847/1538-3881/ae9089)

Fuller note:

## Seventy-two disks, one sequence

The gas that builds a Jupiter does not sit still. It leaves. A paper in The Astronomical Journal, published online on 25 August 2026, uses archival JWST Mid-Infrared Instrument spectra of 72 young, mostly Sun-like stars to watch how it leaves. Naman Bajaj of the University of Arizona led the work. Ilaria Pascucci is the second author. Uma Gorti of the SETI Institute and NASA Ames is a co-author; she has spent years on the theory of disk winds, including photoevaporation.

The sample is the useful part. Each disk is one age and one accretion rate. Lined up, they are frames in a sequence rather than 72 unrelated snapshots.

What they actually counted: extended gas emission in 66 of the 72 disks. Conical molecular-hydrogen winds in 46. Fast neon jets in 40. Every system with a neon jet also showed a wind traced by molecular hydrogen or oxygen. Those are the census numbers. They come from the SETI Institute’s account of the paper, “JWST/MIRI Reveals the Evolution from Molecular to Atomic Disk Winds.”

## Two ways out, and they trade places

In the young systems that are still dumping material onto the star, the spectra are full of magnetically driven jets and winds that carry both molecules and atoms. The picture is a magnetic field threaded through the disk. Gas rides the field lines outward and takes angular momentum with it. The disk can then keep feeding the star, and it also loses mass.

Later, when less material is falling in, the jets weaken. The remaining wind is mostly atomic. High-energy light from the star can get through the thinning gas, heat the disk, and drive it off. That heating-and-escape route is photoevaporation. Ultraviolet and X-rays do the heating. The gas does not need a magnetic slingshot anymore. It is simply warm enough to leave.

A 2020 study led by Pascucci, before JWST could see molecular hydrogen directly, predicted that molecular winds would be there and that they could be thick enough, early on, to block X-rays. Tracing the hydrogen molecule is what let this sample check that prediction. It held.

## The clock is the interpretation

Gorti’s framing, which the SETI piece quotes, is that disk dispersal sets a clock: once the gas is gone, the chance to build a gas-rich planet is over. Bajaj says the same thing more bluntly. A gas giant has to assemble its atmosphere while the disk can still supply it.

Our own system is the local example, offered as context rather than as a new measurement. The Sun is about 4.5 billion years old and the space around it is mostly empty. In the first few million years the disk is thought to have held something like a hundred times more gas than dust. Most of that gas left. The JWST sample is a look at the leaving, across many stars, sorted by age.

The interpretation is the sequence: magnetic jets and molecular winds first, atomic and photoevaporative winds later, and no single process in charge the whole time. The paper does not yet say how many Earth-masses of gas each wind removes, or which radius in the disk the gas comes from. Bajaj’s group lists that as the next measurement. Without it, “race against time” is a fair description of the stakes and a poor description of the schedule. You can see the mechanism change. You cannot yet read a clock face.

An earlier JWST image of gas leaving the disk around T Cha showed the same instruments could do this for one star. Seventy-two stars is what turns a portrait into a trend. The Astronomical Journal paper, DOI 10.3847/1538-3881/ae9089, is the place to check the line measurements. The SETI write-up is the secondary account used here.

### JWST may have found a new kind of object: a black hole wrapped in a star-like cocoon

- Note URL: https://ojaashampiholi.github.io/the-cosmic-notebook/posts/2026-09-01_cosmic-dawn_black-hole-star-mom-bh-1/
- Published: 2026-09-01
- Topics: Black Holes; Cosmology & Early Universe
- Freshness context: Published in Nature on 12 August 2026. The freshness window was expanded from 15 to 30 days because this peer-reviewed result was substantially stronger and more distinct than fresher mission or gallery items.
- Summary: Using the James Webb Space Telescope, astronomers identified an exceptionally red source called MoM-BH*-1 seen about 660 million years after the Big Bang. Its spectrum shows an unusually deep Balmer break and broad hydrogen features that the team models as an actively accreting black hole buried inside an extremely dense, turbulent, dust-free envelope of gas. In the researchers' best-fitting interpretation, the central black hole is about 100,000 times the Sun's mass and the surrounding gas cocoon is roughly the size of the Solar System, so the object looks star-like even though its power source is a black hole rather than nuclear fusion. The authors argue that this configuration could help explain the mysterious 'little red dots' seen by JWST and may reveal a phase in which early black holes grew unusually rapidly.
- Why it matters: Supermassive black holes already existed surprisingly early in cosmic history, and astronomers still do not fully understand how they grew so quickly. MoM-BH*-1 offers direct observational evidence for a long-theorized possibility: a young black hole embedded in very dense gas, potentially allowing rapid growth while also making the object appear dramatically different from a conventional accreting black hole. If similar objects turn out to be common among JWST's little red dots, astronomers may need to revise how they estimate early black-hole masses and how they reconstruct the first stages of galaxy growth.
- Suggested next question: Explore JWST's 'little red dots' and why their strange spectra have become one of the biggest clues to how the first massive black holes formed.
- Explore further: [Nature: A gas-enshrouded and gas-reddened black hole at cosmic dawn](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41586-026-10846-4)
- Sources:
  - [Nature](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41586-026-10846-4)
  - [MIT News](https://news.mit.edu/2026/astronomers-discover-brand-new-type-astrophysical-object-black-hole-star-0812)

Fuller note:

## A red dot that is too bright to be a star

JWST found an exceptionally red source the team calls MoM-BH*-1. In the notebook’s summary of the Nature paper, it is seen about 660 million years after the Big Bang. The spectrum is the awkward part. It shows an unusually deep Balmer break and broad hydrogen features. A Balmer break is a sharp drop in the light below certain wavelengths. Ordinary stellar atmospheres make one. Vega, a bright star in the night sky, shows the familiar version. Rohan Naidu, the lead author, says the break in this object is the deepest they have seen in anything, which is hard to square with a normal star.

There is a second oddity. The light is almost pure hydrogen and helium. Metals, the astronomer’s word for anything heavier, are missing. And the object is violently bright. MIT’s account says it puts out about 100 billion times more energy than any known star can produce by nuclear fusion. Energies like that are routine for a feeding black hole. They are not routine for a star.

Naidu is a NASA Hubble Fellow and Pappalardo Fellow at MIT’s Kavli Institute. Robert Simcoe and Wendy Sun are among the MIT co-authors. They were not hunting a new kind of object. The survey is called Mirage or Miracle, MoM for short, and it was aimed at the earliest galaxies. Naidu’s line on that search is worth keeping: some of what looks like an extremely bright early galaxy, a “miracle,” may be a mirage.

## Dust was the obvious guess. The spectrum refused it.

Very red usually means dust. Smoke reddens a sunset; dust reddens a galaxy. Simcoe says the other signatures did not match a dust screen. The team asked a narrower question: can hydrogen alone, with no dust, make something this red? Their simulations said yes, if the hydrogen is packed so densely that it behaves more like the surface of an enormous star than like a thin nebula.

That dense screen would also soak up blue light and produce a deep Balmer break. It would hide metals if there are hardly any to begin with. It would not, by itself, explain the brightness. Fusion still cannot power it. So they put an accreting black hole in the middle of the hydrogen cocoon and varied the mass until the fake spectrum sat near the real one.

## The fit, and what is still a model

The best-fitting picture, in the paper’s interpretation and in Naidu’s description, is a central black hole of about 100,000 times the Sun’s mass, wrapped in a turbulent, dust-free gas envelope roughly the size of the Solar System. The black hole does the job fusion would do in a star. The gas acts like a fake photosphere. The object looks star-like. The engine is not a star.

Call that the interpretation. The observation is the red, metal-poor spectrum with the extreme break and the luminosity. The black-hole-plus-cocoon arrangement is the scenario that matched the simulations. It is not a photograph of the interior.

The team named it MoM-BH*-1: the survey, plus “black hole star, one.” They suspect it is the first of a class. Little red dots show up across JWST’s deep images and are largely gone in the nearby universe. Naidu argues that every little red dot is consistent with a black hole star sitting inside an ordinary early galaxy, and that MoM-BH*-1 is special because the black hole star outshines the host, so the light is almost uncontaminated. “Consistent with” is not “shown to be.” The dots are fainter than this one. If the same model is later used to weigh them, early black-hole masses could move, and so could the story of how the first galaxies grew. That revision is a possible consequence. It is not yet a required one.

The Nature paper is the authority for the spectral measurements and the model grid. MIT’s write-up is a clear secondary account of the same work. Both leave the little-red-dot population as an argument, which is the right size for the claim.

### Roman launches to map the dark universe and hunt thousands of exoplanets

- Note URL: https://ojaashampiholi.github.io/the-cosmic-notebook/posts/2026-08-31_space-observatory_roman-launches-to-map-the-dark-universe/
- Published: 2026-08-31
- Topics: Telescopes & Observatories; Cosmology & Early Universe; Exoplanets
- Freshness context: NASA announced Roman's successful launch on 30 August 2026, selected within the 15-day freshness window.
- Summary: NASA's Nancy Grace Roman Space Telescope launched successfully on 30 August 2026 and is now traveling toward the Sun-Earth L2 point, about 1.5 million kilometres from Earth. Roman will combine infrared sensitivity and image sharpness comparable to Hubble with a field of view roughly 100 times larger, allowing it to survey enormous areas of the sky far more quickly. Its main science goals include measuring how dark energy has influenced cosmic expansion, mapping dark matter through gravitational lensing, and discovering thousands of exoplanets. NASA says the observatory will spend roughly three months traveling and commissioning before science operations begin, with first public images expected in early 2027.
- Why it matters: Roman is designed to turn questions about dark energy, dark matter, and exoplanet populations into survey-scale measurements, giving astronomers statistical samples far larger than Hubble or Webb can efficiently produce over the same sky area.
- Suggested next question: Explore how gravitational microlensing will let Roman find planets that are difficult to detect with the transit method, including worlds on wide orbits and possibly free-floating planets.
- Explore further: [NASA: Roman Space Telescope launches](https://www.nasa.gov/news-release/nasas-dark-universe-seeking-nancy-grace-roman-space-telescope-launches/)
- Sources:
  - [NASA](https://www.nasa.gov/news-release/nasas-dark-universe-seeking-nancy-grace-roman-space-telescope-launches/)
  - [NASA JPL](https://www.jpl.nasa.gov/news/nasas-dark-universe-seeking-nancy-grace-roman-space-telescope-launches/)

Fuller note:

## A telescope that has left the pad, and not yet started work

NASA says the Nancy Grace Roman Space Telescope launched successfully on 30 August 2026. It is now on its way to the Sun-Earth L2 point, about 1.5 million kilometres from Earth. That is the recorded status. Science operations have not started.

NASA’s account is that Roman will spend roughly three months traveling and being commissioned. First public images are expected in early 2027. Until those images exist, anything said about Roman’s discoveries is a plan, not a result.

The design claim, again from NASA, is specific. Roman is meant to combine infrared sensitivity and image sharpness comparable to Hubble with a field of view roughly 100 times larger. A wide field is the whole point of a survey telescope. Hubble can stare hard at one patch. It cannot cheaply tile the sky. Roman is built to tile.

## Three jobs, none of them finished

NASA lists three main science goals.

One is to measure how dark energy has influenced cosmic expansion. Dark energy is the name for whatever is speeding that expansion up. A survey does not “solve” it. It measures distances and growth across a large sample so the competing descriptions can be told apart.

Another is to map dark matter through gravitational lensing. Mass bends light. If you have sharp images over a huge area, small distortions in the shapes of distant galaxies can be averaged into a map of the mass that did the bending, including mass that does not shine. That sentence is the method. Roman has not delivered the map.

The third is exoplanets, in the thousands. A wide infrared survey can catch many transits, the brief dips when a planet crosses its star. It can also watch for microlensing: a star or planet briefly brightening another star’s light when it passes almost in front. Microlensing is how you find worlds on wide orbits, and planets that are not orbiting a star at all. The notebook’s next question sits there on purpose. Transit surveys are good at close-in planets. They are poor at the ones far out. Roman’s planet haul, if the survey works, should look different from a Kepler-style catalogue because the method is different.

## What would count as success

Hubble and Webb win on depth and on targets someone already cares about. They lose when the scientific question is a rate, a mass function, or a population. Dark energy, dark matter maps, and exoplanet demographics are population questions. You need many objects, measured the same way.

That is the reason Roman matters before it has a single science image. The launch announcement is an engineering fact. The scientific return is still a forecast. Treat NASA’s launch release, and the JPL version of the same announcement, as the authority for the timeline and the stated goals. Papers that use Roman data do not exist yet. When they do, they will replace this note’s description of what the telescope was supposed to do.

### Earth may have repeatedly slipped outside the Sun’s protective bubble

- Note URL: https://ojaashampiholi.github.io/the-cosmic-notebook/posts/earth-heliosphere/
- Published: 2026-08-30
- Topics: Sun & Space Weather; Astrobiology & Habitability
- Freshness context: Research highlighted by NASA on 24 August 2026, with the underlying heliosphere review published in the August 2026 volume of Annual Review of Astronomy and Astrophysics.
- Summary: NASA-funded researchers reconstructed the Sun’s recent journey through the Milky Way and found that it likely encountered dense interstellar cold clouds at least three times in the past 14 million years. During these encounters, surrounding gas may have compressed the heliosphere — the bubble carved out by the solar wind that normally shields the planets — to smaller than Earth’s orbit, temporarily leaving Earth directly exposed to the interstellar environment. The modeled encounters line up with unusual isotopes found in deep-sea sediments, Antarctic material, and lunar samples, and could have altered atmospheric chemistry, radiation exposure, and perhaps ancient climate.
- Why it matters: Earth’s long-term environment depends on its orbit and on the Sun’s activity. It also depends on the Sun’s motion through the Galaxy. That adds an external variable to questions about planetary climate, radiation, habitability, and potentially the evolution of life.
- Suggested next question: Look into the heliosphere and how its size changes as the Solar System moves through different regions of the interstellar medium.
- Explore further: [NASA’s Starstruck research feature](https://science.nasa.gov/solar-system/starstruck-nasa-research-shows-how-suns-ancient-history-shaped-earth/)
- Sources:
  - [NASA Science](https://science.nasa.gov/solar-system/starstruck-nasa-research-shows-how-suns-ancient-history-shaped-earth/)
  - [Annual Reviews](https://www.annualreviews.org/content/journals/10.1146/annurev-astro-120425-053711)

Fuller note:

## Three times the shield shrank past Earth’s orbit

The heliosphere is the bubble the solar wind blows in the interstellar gas. It is not a hard wall. It is the region where the Sun’s outflow still dominates. Spacecraft at the edge have crossed it. Earth, in ordinary times, sits well inside.

NASA’s SHIELD center, a DRIVE science center led by Merav Opher at Boston University, reconstructed the Sun’s recent path through the Milky Way and the clouds it met. The work is in the August 2026 Annual Review of Astronomy and Astrophysics, and NASA highlighted it on 24 August 2026. In the simulations, the Sun ran into dense, cold interstellar clouds at least three times in the past 14 million years. The dates they give are roughly 2 to 3 million years ago, 6 to 7 million, and 13 to 14 million. Each time, the cloud pressed the heliosphere down to smaller than Earth’s orbit. Earth would have been left in interstellar space, still bound to the Sun, no longer inside the solar-wind bubble.

That is the model result. The supporting observation is chemical. Isotopes that are common in interstellar dust and rare in ordinary Earth material show up in deep-sea sediments, Antarctic material, and lunar samples on those same timelines. The match is why the encounters are more than a trajectory drawn on a map of the local galaxy. A cloud that compresses the heliosphere also delivers dust. The archives of that dust are mud, ice, and the Moon.

## What exposure would have changed, and what is still a “could”

Outside the bubble, galactic cosmic rays reach the atmosphere more easily, and the mix of incoming gas changes. The SHIELD simulations follow that into the upper atmosphere: more water vapor, a shift in the dynamics aloft, and, from there, a possible change at the surface. NASA’s feature connects those exposures to ancient climate swings, including ice-age intervals, as a candidate external driver alongside the usual internal ones — orbit, greenhouse gases, ice sheets.

Keep the ranks straight. The path through the clouds, the three compressions, and the isotope coincidences are the findings being reported. A specific ice age caused by a specific cloud is a further interpretation. Opher’s group is offering the heliosphere’s galactic journey as a factor that belongs in the climate conversation. They are not, in the account used here, replacing orbital cycles.

The notebook’s sources are the NASA feature and the Annual Review. The NASA piece also describes a separate study, by Vladimir Airapetian, on the faint young Sun billions of years ago and greenhouse gases sparked by solar particles. That is a different problem and a different paper. It is not this result. This note stays with the last 14 million years and the cold clouds.

## A variable the surface does not advertise

Earth’s habitability is usually discussed with the Sun as a lamp at a fixed distance. The lamp moves through the galaxy. The bubble around the lamp changes size when the neighborhood gets dense. For a few intervals in the recent geological past, “inside the heliosphere” may not have described the planet. Life was already here. The question is what the atmosphere and the radiation dose did, not whether the planet was sterilized. The isotope layers are the place a geologist can test the astronomers. If the layers line up with the simulated dates, the encounters get harder to wave off. If a layer is missing, that date is in trouble.

The Annual Review article is the authority for the trajectory and the heliosphere model. NASA’s write-up is the public account of the same SHIELD work, plus the separate young-Sun study that should not be merged into it. The next object to understand is the heliosphere itself: how far the solar wind reaches, and how fast that reach collapses when a cold cloud arrives.

### Hubble uncovers the Milky Way’s earliest confirmed major merger

- Note URL: https://ojaashampiholi.github.io/the-cosmic-notebook/posts/milky-way-earliest-major-merger/
- Published: 2026-08-29
- Topics: Galaxies & Galactic Evolution
- Freshness context: Published by NASA Hubble on 17 August 2026 and selected within the 15-day freshness window.
- Summary: Hubble observations have helped identify the Milky Way’s earliest confirmed major merger, involving the Low-energy-Kraken-Heracles system. The finding shows that accreted stars from external galaxies were already important during the Galaxy’s earliest growth.
- Why it matters: The finding pushes the Milky Way’s confirmed merger history about 1.8 billion years farther back and shows that accreted stars from external galaxies were already important during the Galaxy’s earliest growth.
- Suggested next question: Explore how globular clusters and their stellar populations preserve evidence of the Milky Way’s early assembly history.
- Explore further: [NASA Hubble: the Milky Way’s early merger](https://science.nasa.gov/missions/hubble/hubble-solves-merger-mystery-from-milky-ways-early-years/)
- Sources:
  - [NASA Hubble](https://science.nasa.gov/missions/hubble/hubble-solves-merger-mystery-from-milky-ways-early-years/)

Fuller note:

## A dwarf galaxy, eaten early, filed under three older names

Hubble has identified the Milky Way’s earliest confirmed major merger. The dwarf is called Low-energy-Kraken-Heracles, LKH for short, after three earlier papers that had argued for an ancient merger without agreeing on the details. The collision was about 11.8 billion years ago, around two billion years after the Big Bang. NASA’s Hubble release, 17 August 2026, says this pushes the confirmed merger history 1.8 billion years farther back than the previous earliest secure event. The paper is in Nature Astronomy. Davide Massari, at the Astrophysics and Space Science Observatory of Bologna, led it.

The Milky Way grew in two ways at once: new stars from its own gas, and stars, gas, and dark matter taken from smaller galaxies. The recent big case is the Sagittarius dwarf, a merger that began more than 6 billion years ago and is still going. Before that, Gaia-Sausage-Enceladus was consumed about 10 billion years ago and did a lot to rearrange the stellar disk. Smaller mergers sit between those two. Both data and simulations had pointed at yet another large merger, earlier still. The arguments were about which clusters, which stars, and whether the evidence had been scrambled away. LKH is that earlier galaxy, now with a clock.

## Globular clusters as the archive

The team used Hubble to study globular clusters, the dense balls of old stars, in the inner 20,000 light-years of the Galaxy. They looked at 39 of them. Clusters keep a record of where they formed because their stars share an age and a metallicity, the proportion of elements heavier than helium. Chiara Zerbinati, a co-author at the University of Bologna, notes that Hubble’s resolution is what made those ages and metallicities precise enough to sort populations that ground data had blurred.

Gaia’s motions supply the other axis. Together, the sample splits into more than the two groups the team expected (clusters born in the young Milky Way, and clusters brought in by Gaia-Sausage-Enceladus). A third population is older than the Gaia-Sausage-Enceladus clusters and younger than the Milky Way’s own, across the range of metallicity. That combination is hard to produce inside one galaxy. It fits clusters born in a separate dwarf and brought in when that dwarf was eaten.

The dwarf’s stellar mass, in the NASA account, was roughly 500 million times the Sun. That is a serious fraction of the Milky Way’s mass at the time, which is why “major” is justified. The Galaxy was smaller then. A partner of that size is not a light snack.

## What “confirmed” changes, and what it does not

Massari’s point is aimed at a specific earlier claim: that the earliest Milky Way was built only from stars born in place. The LKH clusters say accreted stars were already a large ingredient during that first growth. Fernando Aguado-Agelet, a co-author at the Universities of Vigo and La Laguna, frames the follow-up as more clusters, including ones Hubble has not studied, so the later mergers can be put on the same footing.

Confirmed does not mean the whole merger tree is finished. It means this event, at this time, with this mass scale, is no longer only a disputed peak in a simulation or a chemical overdensity. The 1.8 billion years is a comparison with the previous confirmed milestone, not a claim that nothing happened before LKH. Earlier, smaller accretions can still be hiding.

NASA’s release is the public account. Nature Astronomy is the authority for the cluster ages and the population split. The name is a compromise among Kraken, Heracles, and the low-energy merger discussed in the earlier papers, which is itself a hint that the community had pieces of this galaxy already and did not yet have a single object to point at.

### S301: the fastest known star in the Milky Way may reveal Sagittarius A*’s spin

- Note URL: https://ojaashampiholi.github.io/the-cosmic-notebook/posts/s301-sagittarius-a-star-spin/
- Published: 2026-08-28
- Topics: Black Holes; Gravity & Fundamental Physics
- Freshness context: Published by ESO on 19 August 2026 and selected within the 15-day freshness window.
- Summary: S301 is the fastest known star in the Milky Way and passes exceptionally close to Sagittarius A*, the supermassive black hole at the Galactic Centre. Its orbit may be measurably altered by relativistic effects caused by the black hole’s rotation, offering astronomers a new way to probe that spin.
- Why it matters: S301 passes so close to Sagittarius A* that relativistic effects from the black hole’s rotation should measurably alter its orbit, creating a practical new test of strong-field gravity.
- Suggested next question: Explore how the GRAVITY instrument on the Very Large Telescope Interferometer measures stellar orbits near the Galactic Centre.
- Explore further: [ESO: S301 and Sagittarius A*](https://eso.org/public/news/eso2612/)
- Sources:
  - [ESO](https://eso.org/public/news/eso2612/)

Fuller note:

## A star that will feel the twist, and has not yet delivered the number

S301 is the fastest star known in the Milky Way. At its closest pass to Sagittarius A*, the four-million-solar-mass black hole at the Galactic Centre, it moves at about 25,000 kilometres per second. That is a bit over 8 percent of the speed of light. The orbit takes 8.7 years. The closest approach is about 12 times the Earth-Sun distance, 1.78 billion kilometres, only about 20 percent farther than Saturn’s distance from the Sun. No other star yet observed comes in that tight. ESO announced it on 19 August 2026. The paper, from the GRAVITY+ collaboration, is in Nature.

The observations were made with the Very Large Telescope Interferometer at Paranal, combining four 8-metre telescopes. GRAVITY, and the upgraded GRAVITY+, is the instrument. Frank Eisenhauer, the GRAVITY+ principal investigator, notes that no other observatory has four telescopes of that size that can work as one interferometer. The star is about two billion times fainter than Betelgeuse. They first caught it in spring 2023, traced the orbit back to 2017, and found that the last close pass was early 2023. The next one is in 2031.

Felix Mang, a PhD student at the Max Planck Institute for Extraterrestrial Physics and an author of the study, is the person attached to the hope you should not upgrade into a result: within about ten years, this star could yield the spin of Sagittarius A*. Stefan Gillessen, who led much of the work with him, calls that a direct spin measurement and a sharp test of general relativity. It has not been done. One orbit is not enough. They want at least two full, well-sampled orbits so the trajectory is known tightly enough to see the small twist.

## What spin would do, and why this star is the one

A spinning black hole drags spacetime with it. The drag shifts the orbits of nearby stars, more strongly when the star is close and fast. S2 and the other famous Galactic Centre stars were the previous best levers. They are not as close as S301. Juan Osorno, at the Paris Observatory, puts the practical consequence cleanly: without this star, the same spin measurement from the older stars would take several more decades. Reinhard Genzel, whose group’s long campaign of stellar orbits helped establish the black hole, calls S301 a new window on spacetime near Sagittarius A*. The window is open. The measurement is ahead.

The origin story is also an inference, and ESO labels it as one. Stars do not form this close to the black hole. S301’s orbit fits a binary that was torn apart: one star captured onto the tight ellipse, the companion kicked out fast enough that it may have left the Galaxy. “Likely” is the word in the release. It is a good dynamical story. It is not a sighting of the ejected partner.

## Two instruments, one future pass

MICADO, on ESO’s Extremely Large Telescope, is named alongside GRAVITY+ as the follow-up. The 2031 pericentre is the next time the relativistic effects are strongest. Missing it would hurt. Getting it, and the orbit before and after, is the actual experiment. Until that reduction is published, any number quoted as “the spin of Sagittarius A*” did not come from S301.

What is in hand: the star, the speed, the period, the periapsis, the instrument, and a path to a spin measurement that did not exist before this orbit. What is not in hand: the spin. ESO’s release eso2612 is the public account. The Nature paper is the authority for the orbital fit. The notebook’s job is to keep those two lists from collapsing into each other.
